This matters enormously in speech. If you place the accent on the wrong syllable, native speakers may struggle to understand you, even if every single letter you say is technically correct. The rhythmic pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables is what gives speech its natural flow.

Some languages, like English, use what linguists call a stress accent — the accented syllable is louder and longer. Other languages use a pitch accent — the accented syllable is marked by a change in musical pitch rather than volume. Japanese and Mandarin Chinese work this way.
3. A Mark Written on a Letter (Written Language)

An accent can also be a small mark written above, below, or through a letter to show how it should be pronounced. These are called diacritical marks, but in everyday speech, people almost always just call them "accents."

You see these all the time in French, Spanish, Portuguese, German, and many other languages. For example:

The mark over the é in the French word café tells you to pronounce that letter as a sharp, clear "ay" sound rather than a soft or silent one. Without the accent mark, the letter e would be pronounced differently.

In Spanish, the ñ in mañana tells you this is a distinct sound (like "ny") rather than a plain n.

In some words, the accent mark also signals which syllable should be stressed when the word is spoken aloud. In others, it purely marks how a specific letter sounds. The exact role of the mark depends on the language.

In English, accent marks appear mostly in words borrowed from other languages — like naïve, résumé, or façade — and their usage is slowly declining in English writing, though they remain essential in their original languages.
4. Special Emphasis on Something (General / Figurative Meaning)

More broadly, accent can mean special importance or emphasis placed on something — even outside the world of language.

You might read: "The school puts a strong accent on creativity." This simply means the school emphasizes creativity above other things. Or: "The new policy places its accent on fairness." Here, accent is used exactly as the word emphasis or focus would be used. This meaning flows naturally from the linguistic meaning — just as you stress one syllable in a word to make it stand out, you can "accent" something in life to make it the most prominent or important part.

In music, an accent is a mark or instruction telling a musician to play a particular note or beat with extra force or emphasis. When you see an accent mark on a note in sheet music, you play that note louder and more forcefully than the surrounding notes. The result is a slight punch or stress that gives music its rhythmic character and emotional expressiveness. A steady stream of notes played all at the same volume would sound mechanical; accents are what make music feel alive and rhythmic.

In visual arts and interior design, an accent is a small detail or element that stands out from the rest, drawing the eye and adding visual interest. It is something distinctive in an otherwise uniform background.

An accent color in a room is a bold color used in small doses — perhaps a bright red cushion in a room that is otherwise beige — specifically to create contrast and draw attention. An accent wall is one wall painted differently from the others. An accent piece in fashion might be a striking belt or necklace that makes an outfit stand out. In all these cases, the accent is the element that does not blend in — it is the one that announces itself.

All these meanings share the same soul: an accent is whatever stands apart from its surroundings by being given more prominence. A stressed syllable stands out among unstressed ones. A regional accent stands out against other ways of speaking. A written mark distinguishes one letter from another. An accent color pops against the neutral background. A musical accent punches through the surrounding notes.

The word always points to the same thing: the part that rises above the rest.
170:
To accentuate something means to make it more noticeable, more prominent, or more striking than it would otherwise appear. Think of it this way: something already exists — a feature, a quality, a sound, a feeling — and you accentuate it by drawing extra attention to it, making it stand out more clearly against everything around it.

The key idea is emphasis through amplification. You are not creating something new. You are taking something that is already there and turning up its visibility so that it becomes difficult or impossible to ignore. This is what separates accentuate from words like create or produce — the thing being accentuated must already exist; you are simply making it louder, clearer, or more visible.

The word is wonderfully versatile and appears across many areas of life. In fashion and physical appearance, a person might wear a belt to accentuate their waist — the belt does not create the waist, but it draws the eye to it and makes its shape more defined. In speech, a speaker accentuates a word or phrase by saying it louder, slower, or with a deliberate pause before it, ensuring that the listener pays special attention to it. In art and design, a painter might use a burst of bright color to accentuate the focal point of a canvas, or an architect might use lighting to make a particular detail stand out. In everyday situations, you might say that the silence in a room accentuated the tension between two people — meaning the quietness made the tension feel more intense and impossible to ignore.

An important nuance is that the word can work in both positive and negative directions — it is completely neutral and does not judge whether what is being highlighted is something good or something bad. You could say "her warm smile accentuated her kindness," where a positive quality is being made more visible. But you could equally say "the harsh lighting accentuated every flaw on the surface," where an unflattering quality is being made more prominent. Or consider: "the new report only accentuated the depth of the crisis," where a serious problem is being made to feel even more stark and pressing. In all three cases, the word is doing the same job — amplifying what is already there — but what it amplifies can be a strength, a weakness, or a difficulty.

Accentuate is closely related to words like emphasize, highlight, underscore, and stress. However, it carries a slightly richer, more sensory quality. When you emphasize something, you usually do so through words or argument — you tell someone what matters. When you accentuate something, there is more of a sense that you are shaping perception — making something stand out through contrast, design, tone, or visual framing, rather than just pointing it out. Accentuate tends to suggest a more deliberate crafting of how something is perceived by others.

A helpful way to internalize this word is to imagine a musician performing a quiet, gentle piece — and then, at a precise moment, striking one single note much harder and louder than all the others. That note is accentuated. The contrast with everything around it is what gives it its power. This is the spirit of the word across all its uses: through deliberate choice and contrast, you make one thing rise above its surroundings and demand to be noticed.

Finally, the most famous phrase using this word is "accentuate the positive," which means to focus on and highlight what is good rather than dwelling on what is bad. This phrase captures something true about the word itself — to accentuate is to shine a light on something, to bring it forward, to make it more present in the mind of whoever is watching or listening. And because whatever you accentuate gets more of the world's attention, the choice of what to accentuate — and what to quietly leave in the background — is itself a meaningful and deliberate act.
171:
Accept means to take something in or agree to something willingly. The key word here is willingly. You are not forced. You are not tricked. You choose to receive it, believe it, or say yes to it.

This one word actually does several related jobs depending on the situation.

1. To receive something that is offered to you

When someone gives or offers you something — a gift, money, food, help — and you take it without refusing, you accept it.

She accepted the flowers he gave her.
He accepted the money gratefully.
The charity accepts donations from the public.

Notice that the opposite here is to refuse or reject. If you don't want something and you push it away, you reject it. If you take it willingly, you accept it.

2. To say yes to an offer, invitation, or proposal

When someone asks you to do something — come to a party, take a job, marry them — and you agree, you accept their offer or invitation.

She accepted the job offer.
He accepted the invitation to the wedding.
They accepted the terms of the contract.

Here, the opposite is to decline or turn down. When you accept an offer, you are saying: "Yes, I agree to this."

3. To believe or recognize something as true or valid

When you accept a fact, an idea, or someone's explanation, you are saying that you believe it is true and you are no longer questioning it.

Scientists accept that the Earth orbits the Sun.
The jury accepted his explanation.
He refused to accept that he was wrong.

This is different from just hearing something. You could hear an idea and still reject it. When you accept it, you take it in as truth.

4. To come to terms with something difficult — stop fighting it mentally

This is one of the deepest and most emotionally powerful uses of the word. When something painful or unchangeable happens — a loss, a failure, a harsh reality — and you stop fighting it in your mind, stop denying it, and finally make peace with it, you accept it.

After years of struggling, he finally accepted that his marriage was over.
She slowly accepted the fact that she had not been chosen.
Accepting failure is the first step toward growth.

Notice the difference from the previous meaning: believing a fact (meaning 3) is about truth. Accepting a difficult reality (meaning 4) is about your emotional and psychological response. You might already know something is true but still not have accepted it — you're still in denial, still fighting it inside. Acceptance here means letting go of that inner resistance.

5. To welcome someone into a group, community, or role

When a school, company, club, or group of people decide to include someone, they accept them. This means they are letting the person in and treating them as belonging.

She was accepted into medical school.
The new boy was finally accepted by his classmates.
He was accepted as a full member of the team.

The opposite here is reject. Being rejected means being left out; being accepted means being let in.

6. To take on or own a responsibility, consequence, or outcome

When you willingly take ownership of something — whether it's blame, a challenge, a consequence, or a result — you accept it. You are not avoiding it or passing it to someone else.

He accepted full responsibility for the error.
She accepted the consequences of her choice.
The general accepted defeat.
He accepted the challenge without fear.
What All These Meanings Have in Common

Every use of accept shares one thing: willingness without force.

  • You are not just receiving — you are choosing to receive.
  • You are not just hearing something — you are taking it in as real or valid.
  • You are not just told you belong somewhere — you are welcomed.

This is why "accept" feels warmer and more active than neutral words like "get" or "receive." It always implies that you are opening the door.

Understanding these distinctions will sharpen your use of the word greatly.

Accept vs. Receive
Receive is neutral — it just means something came to you. You can receive bad news, a punch, a cold. There's no choice involved. Accept always implies you chose to take it. You might receive a gift but refuse to accept it (you push it back). You receive rain whether you like it or not; you can never truly "accept" rain in this sense — you can only accept that rainy days exist.

Accept vs. Agree
Agree is specifically about sharing an opinion or giving consent to a plan. Accept is broader — you can accept a gift (not about agreement), accept someone into a team (not about opinions), or accept a fact (which is closer to agreement but not quite the same). Every time you agree with someone, there's an element of acceptance, but not every acceptance is an agreement.

Accept vs. Acknowledge
Acknowledge means you recognize that something exists or is true — but it's more surface level. You can acknowledge a problem and still not truly accept it. Acknowledgement says: "I see this." Acceptance says: "I take this in and I stop resisting it." A person might acknowledge that they have a bad habit (they admit it exists) but not accept it (they haven't made peace with it or decided to own it).

Accept vs. Admit
Admit often carries a feeling of reluctance — you are confessing something you'd rather keep hidden or not face. Accept is more neutral to positive. You admit you made a mistake (a bit uncomfortable); you accept the consequences of that mistake (you take them on). You would rarely say "I admit the gift" but you would say "I accept the gift."
Important Patterns and How to Use It

Accept + a noun

This is the most common pattern. The noun is the thing being taken in or agreed to.

accept an offer / an invitation / a gift / a challenge / payment / criticism / responsibility / defeat / blame

Accept + that (+ a sentence)

When accepting a fact or reality, you often follow it with that and a full thought.

I finally accepted that I couldn't do everything alone.
She couldn't accept that he was gone.
He accepted that he had lost.

Accept + someone (for who they are)

When accepting a person — not just into a group, but as they truly are — this phrase is very common.

Her family finally accepted her for who she is.
A good friend accepts you without trying to change you.

"This machine accepts..."

Objects and systems can also "accept" things in the sense that they are designed to take them in.

This ATM accepts all major cards.
The form accepts only numbers in this field.
The website accepts applications until December.

Here it's not about emotion or willingness — it's about what the system is built to receive.
A Few Sentences Showing the Full Range

SituationExample
  • Receiving willingly: He accepted the award on behalf of his team.
  • Agreeing to an offer: She accepted the proposal and said yes.
  • Believing as true: Most people now accept that the climate is changing.
  • Making peace with reality: It took him years to accept that his father was never coming back.
  • Welcoming into a group: He was accepted into the most competitive program in the country.
  • Taking responsibility: She accepted the blame without any excuses.
  • A system taking input: The vending machine only accepts exact change.
One Sentence to Remember It All

If you ever forget everything else, hold onto this:

To accept something is to open yourself to it — willingly, without fighting it away.

Whether it's a gift, a truth, a person, or a painful reality — when you accept it, you stop pushing it away and let it in.
172:
Acceptance means receiving, agreeing to, or making peace with something — whether that's an offer, an idea, a person, or a painful reality. It is the state of saying "yes" rather than "no," of letting something in rather than pushing it away.

Think of it as the opposite of rejection. When you reject something, you push it away. When you accept something, you let it in.

The word carries several closely related but distinct shades of meaning depending on the context.

Receiving something offered. The most straightforward meaning. When someone offers you a gift, a job, an invitation, or a proposal and you say yes, that act of saying yes is acceptance. "His acceptance of the job offer surprised everyone."

Agreeing that something is true or valid. Acceptance can also mean acknowledging that a fact, belief, or idea is real or correct. "There is wide acceptance among scientists that the climate is changing."

Being welcomed into a group. This is the social meaning of the word. When the people around you include you, welcome you, and treat you as one of their own, you experience acceptance. This is one of the deepest human needs. "She finally found acceptance among her new friends."

Coming to peace with something difficult. This is perhaps the most profound meaning of the word. When something painful or unchangeable happens in your life — a loss, a failure, a personal limitation — acceptance is the state of no longer fighting against it. It means you have stopped denying reality and made peace with things as they are, even if you don't like them. "After years of grief, he finally reached acceptance of his father's death."

Formal agreement. In legal, business, or institutional contexts, acceptance is the official act of agreeing to terms, an offer, or an application. "Acceptance of the contract makes it legally binding." This is also why a university sends you an acceptance letter — it is the official confirmation that your application has been approved.
What Acceptance Is NOT — The Crucial Distinctions

This is where most people get confused, so pay close attention.

Acceptance is not the same as approval. Approval means you think something is good or right. Acceptance simply means you acknowledge it and stop resisting it. A parent might accept that their adult child has made a poor decision, without approving of that decision. These are two completely different things.

Acceptance is not the same as agreement. You can accept a situation without thinking it is fair or correct. If a group makes a decision you disagree with, you might accept it and move forward without ever agreeing that it was the right call.

Acceptance is not the same as happiness. Especially in the emotional sense, acceptance does not mean you feel good about something. It simply means you have stopped pretending it isn't real. A person can accept a terminal diagnosis and still feel deep sadness, fear, or anger. Acceptance is not about feeling good — it is about facing the truth without hiding from it.

Acceptance is not giving up. Accepting a difficult reality doesn't make you passive or mean you stop trying to change things. You can fully accept that a serious problem exists and still work hard to solve it. In fact, accepting a problem clearly is often the first step to solving it.
Common Phrases Built Around This Word

Acceptance letter — A formal written notification, usually from a college or university, telling you that your application has been approved and you have a place there.

Acceptance speech — The speech someone gives when receiving an award or honor. When an actor wins an Oscar and thanks everyone on stage, that is an acceptance speech.

Self-acceptance — Accepting yourself as you are, with your strengths and your flaws, without harsh judgment. It does not mean you stop trying to grow; it means you are not at war with yourself.

Conditional acceptance — Acceptance that comes with specific conditions. For example, a university might offer you conditional acceptance, meaning you are admitted only if you meet certain requirements.

Blanket acceptance — Accepting everything all at once, without questioning the individual parts.

Understanding the words close to acceptance will sharpen your understanding of the word itself.

Approval is stronger. It means you actively think something is good or right. Acceptance is more neutral — you can accept something without approving of it.

Acknowledgment is weaker. You might acknowledge that something exists without truly accepting it. Acknowledgment is just recognizing a fact; acceptance means you've come to terms with it.

Tolerance is close, but it carries a slight edge of discomfort. You tolerate something you don't particularly like. Acceptance suggests a greater degree of peace.

Agreement is about sharing an opinion. Acceptance is broader — you can accept a situation without agreeing it is right or fair.

Recognition simply means noticing or identifying something. It is much less emotional and personal than acceptance.

Rejection is the direct opposite — pushing something away instead of letting it in.

Refusal is saying no to something offered.

Denial is refusing to acknowledge a reality, especially a painful one. Where acceptance means turning to face the truth, denial means turning away from it.

Resistance is actively fighting against something rather than making peace with it.
One Simple Way to Remember It

If rejection is closing a door, acceptance is opening it.
If denial is turning your back on the truth, acceptance is turning to face it.

At its deepest level, acceptance means: "I am not pushing this away. I am allowing it to be real."

That single idea — allowing something to be real — runs through every meaning of the word, from accepting a job offer to accepting a loss. The context changes; the core does not.
173:
An acceptance letter is an official written document in which one party says "Yes, I agree" to another party. It is a formal way of confirming that you have received an offer — whether that offer is a job, a place at a university, a business deal, or a proposal — and that you are willingly and clearly agreeing to it.

Think of it like this: imagine someone offers you a seat at their dinner table. An acceptance letter is your polite, written, and official way of saying, "Thank you, I'll be there." But in the real world, that "seat" could be a job, a college admission, or a contract — and the stakes are much higher, so the confirmation needs to be in writing.
Why a Written Letter? Why Not Just Say Yes?

Spoken agreements can be forgotten, misunderstood, or denied later. A written acceptance letter creates a permanent record that both sides can refer back to. It protects both the person making the offer and the person accepting it. It says, clearly and without confusion: "We both agreed to this, on this date, under these terms."
The Two Sides of Every Acceptance Letter

Every acceptance letter exists within a relationship between two parties:

The Offerer — the person or organization who made the offer (a company, a university, a landlord, a business partner).

The Accepter — the person who received the offer and is now writing the acceptance letter to confirm their agreement.

The acceptance letter always travels from the accepter to the offerer.

Acceptance letters appear in many areas of life. Here are the most common ones:

1. College or University Admissions
When a student applies to a university and gets selected, the university sends the student an admission acceptance letter. This tells the student that they have been officially admitted. The student may then write their own acceptance letter back, confirming that they accept the seat offered to them.

2. Job Offers
When a company offers someone a job, they usually send a formal job offer letter. The candidate then writes an acceptance letter to confirm they are taking the job. This letter signals the beginning of a professional relationship.

3. Business and Contracts
When two businesses negotiate a deal, one party may send a proposal. The other party responds with an acceptance letter, agreeing to the terms. This can have legal significance, as it can mark the moment a binding contract is formed.

4. Scholarships and Fellowships
When a scholarship-granting body selects a recipient, they send a notification. The recipient writes an acceptance letter to formally confirm they will use the scholarship.

5. Real Estate and Housing
When a landlord approves a tenant's rental application, an acceptance letter may be issued confirming the approval and the terms of the tenancy.
What an Acceptance Letter Typically Contains

While the exact content depends on the situation, most acceptance letters share these common elements:

A clear statement of acceptance — This is the heart of the letter. It directly and unambiguously states that the offer is being accepted. There should be no room for doubt.

Reference to the original offer — The letter mentions the specific offer being accepted, often including the date of the original offer, the position or program, and any other identifying details. This ensures both parties are talking about the same thing.

Gratitude or acknowledgment — Most acceptance letters express thanks or acknowledge the opportunity being given. This is a professional courtesy.

Confirmation of key terms — In many cases, especially in job or business contexts, the letter restates the key terms of the offer — such as salary, start date, or conditions — to confirm that both parties have the same understanding.

The writer's signature and date — Since this is an official document, it is signed and dated to make it valid and traceable.
Acceptance Letter vs. Offer Letter — What's the Difference?

These two are often confused, so let's clear it up simply:

An offer letter comes first — it is sent by the offerer to the accepter. It lays out what is being offered.

An acceptance letter comes second — it is sent by the accepter back to the offerer. It confirms the agreement.

One presents the opportunity; the other locks it in.
Acceptance Letter vs. Acknowledgment Letter — What's the Difference?

An acknowledgment letter simply says, "I received your offer and I'm looking at it." It does not say yes or no.

An acceptance letter goes further — it clearly says, "I received your offer, and my answer is YES."
The Legal Weight of an Acceptance Letter

In many situations, an acceptance letter is not just a formality — it can be legally binding. In contract law, an agreement is generally formed when a valid offer is met with a clear and unconditional acceptance. An acceptance letter can serve as the written proof of that moment of agreement.

For this reason, it is important to read an offer carefully before writing an acceptance letter. Once you formally accept, you may be legally obligated to follow through on your commitment. If you later back out, there could be professional or legal consequences depending on the nature of the agreement.
Key Qualities of a Good Acceptance Letter

Clarity — It must be absolutely clear that you are accepting. Vague or hesitant language weakens it.

Promptness — Most offers come with a deadline. Responding in a timely manner is both respectful and practical.

Professionalism — Even if the context is informal, keeping a respectful and professional tone is important.

Accuracy — If you are restating any terms from the original offer, make sure you state them correctly to avoid misunderstandings later.

Conciseness — A good acceptance letter is thorough but not unnecessarily long. It says what needs to be said and stops there.
A Simple Way to Remember It

An acceptance letter = Your formal, written "YES" to an offer.

It is the document that closes the gap between being offered something and officially committing to it. Whether it's your dream job, your university of choice, or a business deal, the acceptance letter is the moment where possibility becomes reality — on paper, on the record, and often, under the law.
174:
Accessible means able to be reached, entered, used, or understood — without significant barriers.

Think of a barrier as anything that stops you or makes it hard for you to get to, into, or through something. When a barrier is removed or absent, the thing becomes accessible. That's the soul of this word.

1. Physically Accessible — you can reach or enter a place or thing

This is the most literal sense. A place is physically accessible when your body can reach or get into it without difficulty.

The mountain trail is accessible only during summer months — it's blocked by snow the rest of the year.

The new library building is accessible to wheelchair users, with ramps, wide doors, and lifts.

Here, the barrier is physical — terrain, locked doors, stairs, distance, or geography. When those barriers don't exist (or are removed), the place is called accessible.

This sense also applies to objects:

Keep the fire extinguisher in an accessible spot — don't hide it behind furniture.

Notice: the word doesn't just mean "you can get to it" — it also carries a sense of ease. Something is accessible when getting to it doesn't require unusual effort.

2. Available or Obtainable — you can get hold of it

Sometimes the barrier is not physical but about whether something is available to you at all — whether it exists within your reach.

Clean drinking water is not accessible to millions of people around the world.

The documents are accessible to employees with a security clearance.

With the internet, information that was once locked in university libraries is now accessible to anyone.

In these cases, "accessible" means within reach in a broader sense — it exists and you are permitted or able to obtain it. The barrier might be legal, political, economic, or practical.

3. Intellectually Accessible — easy to understand

This is one of the most important and widely used senses today. When ideas, writing, art, or information are described as accessible, it means they can be understood by a wide audience — not just by experts or specialists.

The professor wrote an accessible book on quantum physics — even a curious teenager could follow it.

His lectures are very accessible. He avoids jargon and uses simple examples.

Abstract modern art is often criticised for not being accessible to ordinary people.

The barrier here is intellectual: complexity, jargon, assumed prior knowledge, or obscure style. When that barrier is lowered — through clear writing, simple language, good examples — the content becomes accessible.

Important nuance: Saying something is "accessible" does NOT mean it is shallow, dumbed-down, or low quality. It means the author has done the hard work of making something genuinely complex easy to approach without stripping away its depth. This is actually considered a skill and a virtue.

Contrast:

  • Inaccessible writing = dense, full of jargon, hard to follow, assumes too much.
  • Accessible writing = clear, well-explained, welcoming to newcomers — without being simplified to the point of being inaccurate.

4. Accessible in the Sense of Affordable or Within Economic Reach

When the barrier is cost, accessible means something is affordable or available to a wide range of people — not just the wealthy.

The goal of the project is to make quality healthcare accessible to low-income families.

Electric vehicles are becoming more accessible as prices drop.

Luxury goods are, by design, not accessible to most people.

This sense blends with the "obtainable" sense above, but the emphasis here is specifically on price or economic barriers.

5. Accessible — easy to approach (about people)

When used to describe a person — especially someone in a position of authority or fame — accessible means they are easy to talk to, approachable, and not distant or intimidating.

What I admire most about our manager is that she's incredibly accessible — you can walk into her office with any concern.

Despite being a Nobel laureate, he remained accessible to students and never made them feel unwelcome.

The new president promised to be more accessible to the public than his predecessor.

Here, the barrier is social or psychological — a sense of distance, intimidation, or formality. An accessible person removes that barrier; they make themselves easy to reach.

6. Designed for People with Disabilities (Formal / Technical Sense)

In specific formal contexts — architecture, design, technology, law — accessible has a precise technical meaning: designed or adapted so that people with physical, sensory, or cognitive disabilities can use it.

The website must be accessible — it should work with screen readers for visually impaired users.

All new public buildings must meet accessible design standards under the law.

The museum made its exhibitions accessible by adding audio guides, braille labels, and tactile exhibits.

This sense is sometimes called accessibility as a field, and it is taken very seriously in design, technology, and urban planning. An accessible website, for example, works for people who are blind, deaf, have motor disabilities, or have cognitive differences. An accessible building has ramps, lifts, and wide doorways.

This is a specialised use of the same core idea: remove the barriers that prevent certain people from reaching or using something.

No matter which sense you're using, the underlying idea is always the same:

Something is accessible when the barriers between a person and that thing — physical, intellectual, economic, social, legal, or disability-related — are absent or have been removed.

Flip the word: something is inaccessible when those barriers exist and stop people from reaching, using, or understanding it.

Accessible is not just a yes-or-no quality. It exists on a spectrum, and you'll often see it modified:

  • "easily accessible" — almost no barrier at all
  • "readily accessible" — available without delay or difficulty
  • "barely accessible" — technically reachable but with considerable effort
  • "not easily accessible" — significant barriers exist
  • "largely inaccessible" — mostly out of reach for most people
Common Collocations (Words You'll Often See with "Accessible")

• accessible to — accessible to the public, accessible to people with disabilities, accessible to beginners
  • make accessible — the government wants to make education more accessible
  • widely accessible — information is now widely accessible online
  • publicly accessible — a publicly accessible park or database
  • accessible design / accessible format — designed with inclusivity in mind
  • accessible language / accessible writing — easy to understand
Accessible describes something — a place, thing, idea, person, or resource — that can be reached, entered, obtained, understood, or used without significant barriers standing in the way.
175:
The word accessory describes something — or someone — that plays a supporting, secondary role. An accessory is not the main thing. It exists alongside the main thing, helping it, completing it, or enhancing it — but it is never the central focus.

This one idea branches into two very different areas of life: everyday objects and law.

In everyday life, an accessory is an object that is not essential on its own, but adds to the usefulness, beauty, or completeness of something else.

The "something else" is the main item. The accessory is the add-on.

Examples:

  • Fashion: A handbag, a belt, a scarf, sunglasses, or a piece of jewelry worn alongside an outfit. The outfit is the main thing; these items complement it.
  • Technology: A phone case, a charger, a pair of earphones, or a screen protector for your phone. Your phone works without them, but they enhance or protect it.
  • Car: Floor mats, a GPS mount, seat covers. The car runs perfectly without these — they are extras.
  • Camera: A tripod, a lens filter, a camera bag. The camera takes photos; these items support that process.

The key test: If you removed the accessory, the main thing would still function. The accessory adds to it, but the main thing doesn't depend on it to exist or work. A handbag is not part of your clothing — it's an addition. A phone case doesn't make your phone work — it protects it. That "addition, not necessity" quality is what makes something an accessory.

In retail and fashion, the word is used so commonly that entire sections of stores are labelled "Accessories" — meaning the supplementary, add-on items that go with your main purchase or outfit.
Meaning 2: A Person Who Assists in a Crime (Legal)

In law, an accessory is a person who helps or supports someone who commits a crime, without being the person who actually carried out the crime themselves.

The person who directly commits the crime is called the principal. The accessory is the one who plays a supporting role — before, during, or after the crime.

Law recognises two specific types:

Accessory Before the Fact

This is a person who helps prepare or plan a crime before it happens, but is not physically present when the crime is actually committed.

Example: Imagine a robbery is being planned. One person gathers information about when the bank's security is weakest and shares it with the robbers, but stays home on the day of the robbery. That person never entered the bank, never held a weapon — yet they enabled the crime by helping plan it. They are an accessory before the fact.

Other examples of what makes someone an accessory before the fact:

  • Providing a weapon to someone, knowing they plan to use it in a crime
  • Teaching someone a skill specifically for the purpose of committing a crime
  • Financing or funding a criminal act
  • Giving inside information to someone planning to steal from a workplace

The defining features: the help happens before the crime, and the person is absent when it occurs.

Accessory After the Fact

This is a person who helps a criminal after the crime has already been committed, knowing that the crime took place.

Example: A person commits a murder and flees. Their friend knows what happened and hides them in their home, lies to the police about their whereabouts, and helps them escape to another city. The friend did not commit the murder — but they knowingly helped the murderer avoid justice. They are an accessory after the fact.

Other examples of what makes someone an accessory after the fact:

  • Destroying evidence (deleting files, burning clothes, getting rid of a weapon)
  • Providing a false alibi to the police
  • Giving money to a criminal so they can flee
  • Helping a criminal hide or escape

The defining features: the help happens after the crime, and the person knows a crime was committed. If someone unknowingly helps a criminal (say, they genuinely didn't know their friend was a wanted person), they are generally not considered an accessory.
Accessory vs. Accomplice — What's the Difference?

These two words are often confused. Here is the distinction:

  • An accomplice is present and actively participates in the crime as it happens. They are a co-criminal in the act itself.
  • An accessory (especially before or after the fact) is typically not present at the scene. Their involvement is indirect — planning, supporting, or covering up.

Think of it this way: if two people break into a house together, both are accomplices. But if one person stayed outside and kept watch while the other went in, legal systems may treat the lookout differently — as an accessory. And the person who helped the burglars plan the break-in two days earlier, from home, is an accessory before the fact.

(Note: Different countries and legal systems draw these lines slightly differently, but this is the general distinction.)
The Thread That Connects Both Meanings

Whether you're talking about a handbag or a person who helped cover up a crime, the word "accessory" always carries the same underlying idea: secondary, supporting, not the main actor.

  • A scarf is secondary to the outfit.
  • A phone case is secondary to the phone.
  • An accessory to a crime is secondary to the person who committed it.

The word signals: this is not the central thing, but it is connected to it and plays a real role.

• "Accessories to a crime" — people who helped in a crime without being the main criminal
  • "Accessory to murder / robbery / fraud" — specifies what crime they assisted with
  • "Fashion accessories" — supplementary clothing items
  • "Phone accessories" / "car accessories" — add-on products for a device or vehicle
  • "Charged as an accessory" — a legal phrase meaning someone has been accused of helping a criminal

ContextWhat "accessory" means
Everyday objectsA supplementary item that adds to, enhances, or completes a main object
Law (before the fact)A person who helped plan a crime before it happened, but wasn't there
Law (after the fact)A person who helped a criminal after the crime, knowing what happened

The word "accessory" always points to something on the side — never at the centre, but genuinely connected to what is.
176:
When you do something accidentally, you did it without meaning to. You did not plan it. You did not want it to happen. It happened by chance, through a mistake, or through some unforeseen cause — not through your conscious choice.

Think of it this way: your mind had one intention, but the real world produced a different outcome.

"She accidentally knocked over the glass."

— She didn't want to knock it over. Her hand moved in a way she didn't fully control or predict, and it fell.

"Accidentally" is an adverb, which means it describes a verb — it tells you how an action happened. Specifically, it tells you that the action happened without intention.

"He accidentally sent the email to his boss instead of his friend."
"I accidentally deleted the file."
"The child accidentally broke the vase."

In each case, "accidentally" is answering the question: Was this done on purpose? And the answer is: No, it was not.

Understanding "accidentally" fully means seeing three ideas layered inside it:

1. No intention
The person did not plan or want the action or its outcome. This is the most important layer. There was no deliberate decision to cause what happened.

2. Unexpectedness
The outcome came as a surprise — either to the person who caused it, or to others watching, or both.

3. A cause still exists
Something caused it to happen — a slip, a distraction, a moment of carelessness, a coincidence — but that cause was not deliberate choice. This is what separates "accidentally" from things that happen purely on their own (like rain falling).

"He accidentally stepped on the cat."

— He was walking. He wasn't watching carefully. His foot came down on the cat. He caused it — but he did not intend it.
Does It Always Mean Something Bad Happened?

Mostly, yes — but not always. "Accidentally" is often used when something unfortunate, harmful, or regrettable happened without intent. However, it can also describe lucky or positive surprises.

"She accidentally found a $500 note inside an old book." — Lucky!
"Scientists accidentally discovered penicillin." — A great medical breakthrough!

The common thread is not "bad outcome" but rather "unplanned outcome." The word is neutral about whether the result is good or bad — it only tells you about the lack of intention.

That said, when good things happen accidentally, people often call them "happy accidents" or "lucky discoveries," because the word "accidentally" carries a slightly more negative flavour in everyday use.
Does It Mean the Person Is Not at Fault?

Not completely. "Accidentally" reduces blame because it signals the person didn't intend the harm — but it does not erase responsibility.

Consider: "He accidentally spilled hot coffee on her." — He didn't want to, but if he was being careless, he may still owe her an apology or compensation.

In law and ethics, the distinction between intentional and accidental matters enormously — intentional harm is punished more severely than accidental harm. But "accidentally" doesn't mean "no responsibility at all."
How It Compares to Similar Words

These words are close in meaning but differ in important ways:

Accidentally vs. Mistakenly
"Mistakenly" focuses on an error in thinking, believing, or judging.
"Accidentally" focuses on an unintended physical or behavioural outcome.

"I mistakenly believed he was my friend." — A wrong belief.
"I accidentally broke his phone." — An unintended action.

Sometimes they overlap: "I accidentally/mistakenly deleted the file" — both work here because it was both an unintended action and an error in what you did.

Accidentally vs. Unintentionally
These two are very close in meaning. "Unintentionally" is more formal and purely emphasises the absence of intent. "Accidentally" is broader — it also carries the sense of chance and unexpectedness, and is more natural in everyday speech.

"He unintentionally offended her." — Slightly more formal, focuses on the lack of intent.
"He accidentally offended her." — More natural in conversation, same core meaning.

Accidentally vs. Inadvertently
"Inadvertently" is formal and specifically means "without paying attention" — through inattentiveness or oversight.

"She inadvertently revealed the surprise." — She wasn't paying attention to what she was saying.

"Accidentally" is broader — it includes things that happen even when you are paying attention (like an accidental scientific discovery).

Accidentally vs. By Accident
These mean exactly the same thing. "By accident" is the prepositional phrase form of the same idea.

"I met her accidentally." = "I met her by accident."

Use whichever sounds more natural in the sentence.
Where It Sits in a Sentence

"Accidentally" most naturally sits just before the main verb:

"She accidentally spilled the coffee."
"He accidentally deleted the whole folder."

It can also appear at the start of a sentence for emphasis:

"Accidentally, I sent the wrong file."

Or at the end, often with a pause:

"She broke his trust, accidentally."

All three positions are correct. The most common in everyday English is before the verb.

"Accidentally" pairs naturally with verbs like:

  • break, spill, drop, hit, knock over — physical damage
  • delete, send, save, click — digital mistakes
  • reveal, tell, mention — unintended disclosures
  • find, discover, meet — unplanned positive events
  • step on, bump into, touch — unintended physical contact
  • start, trigger, cause — unintended consequences

"Accidentally" is a word about the gap between what you meant to do and what actually happened. Human beings are intentional creatures — we usually act on purpose. But sometimes, actions slip out of our control, or outcomes emerge that we never planned. That is the space "accidentally" lives in.

It is not about being stupid, careless, or negligent (though those things might be part of the story). It is purely about the relationship between your intent and the outcome: if you didn't mean it to happen, it happened accidentally.
177:
Acclaim means enthusiastic, widespread public praise and admiration that people express for someone or something — usually in response to an outstanding achievement, an impressive performance, or a remarkable creation.

It is not a quiet, private compliment. It is loud, open, and shared by many. When a film is released and critics everywhere call it brilliant, audiences celebrate it, and the general public buzzes with admiration — that film has received acclaim.
The Three Pillars of This Word

To truly understand acclaim, remember that it almost always involves all three of these qualities together:

Public — It comes from an audience: critics, the public, experts, or crowds. A friend telling you privately that your painting is great is not acclaim.

Enthusiastic — It is stronger than mild, polite approval. There is real excitement and admiration behind it. People are not just nodding — they are celebrating.

Widespread — It comes from many people, not just one. The more people share the praise, the more fitting it is to call it acclaim.

Acclaim sits well above everyday praise. Compare these two sentences:

  • "People said the book was good."
  • "The book received acclaim."

The first is mild and ordinary. The second tells you that many people are enthusiastically celebrating the book — that it has made a genuine, powerful impression. There is also a sense that the praise is deserved. Acclaim does not feel hollow or exaggerated; it feels earned.

In real writing, acclaim almost always appears with words that tell you how much of it there is or who is giving it:

Critical acclaim — praise specifically from critics, reviewers, and experts in a field.
Popular acclaim — praise from the general public, ordinary people.
Universal acclaim — praise from virtually everyone; almost no one disagrees.
Widespread acclaim — praise from a large number of people.
International acclaim — recognition that has crossed borders and spread across countries.
National acclaim — recognition within a country.

You will also commonly see: "won acclaim," "received acclaim," "earned acclaim," "rose to acclaim," and "met with acclaim."

Acclaim appears most often in the context of:

Art, film, literature, and music — "Her debut album received universal acclaim."
Performances by actors, musicians, or athletes — "He gave a performance that earned him critical acclaim."
Scientific or academic achievements — "Her research brought her international acclaim."
Public figures who have made a major impact — "The leader was met with popular acclaim after the historic speech."
How It Differs From Similar Words

Several words sit near acclaim in meaning, but each has a different shade:

Praise is the broadest and most common word for saying something positive about someone. Acclaim is a stronger, more public, and more enthusiastic version of praise.

Applause is often literal — people physically clapping. Acclaim is broader and more figurative; you do not need a physical audience for acclaim to exist.

Recognition is about acknowledging someone's value or achievement. It can be quiet and neutral. Acclaim adds warmth, enthusiasm, and celebration that recognition does not always carry.

Adulation is more extreme than acclaim. It borders on excessive devotion or worship, often to a degree that feels out of proportion. Acclaim feels earned and proportionate; adulation can feel like blind idolisation.

Plaudits is an older, more formal plural noun that also means enthusiastic praise. It is rarely used in everyday modern writing. Acclaim is far more common.

The natural opposites of acclaim include criticism, condemnation, scorn, derision, and disapproval — when the public or critics express strongly negative judgements about something instead of praising it.

Here are sentences showing the word used naturally, so you can see exactly how it behaves:

"The young architect's first major building was met with widespread acclaim."
— Many people enthusiastically praised her building.

"Despite years of hard work, the composer only received acclaim late in his life."
— Recognition and public praise came to him very late.

"The film earned critical acclaim but struggled to find a popular audience."
— Critics loved it, but regular audiences did not respond as warmly.

"Her speech drew acclaim from people across the political spectrum."
— Even people with different views praised her enthusiastically.

"He had always craved acclaim, but when it finally came, it felt hollow."
— He had always wanted public praise and admiration, but it did not satisfy him as he expected.
If you ever need to recall this word quickly: acclaim is the enthusiastic, public praise that many people give to someone or something truly impressive.
178:
To acclaim someone or something means to praise them openly, enthusiastically, and with great admiration — usually in front of others or as part of a shared public response.

It is not quiet, private, or polite praise. It is loud, strong, and collective. Think of a crowd rising to their feet to cheer for a performer, or the entire world of critics agreeing that a book is a masterpiece. That kind of powerful, shared, public approval is what acclaim captures.

"The audience acclaimed the pianist after her breathtaking performance."

The verb carries two closely related but slightly different uses:

1. To praise with great enthusiasm
This is the most common use. A group of people — critics, audiences, the public — express strong admiration for someone or something.

"The film was acclaimed by critics worldwide."
"Fans acclaimed the new album as her best work yet."

2. To declare or hail someone as something
Here, acclaim means to publicly announce or recognize someone as holding a title, status, or role — done with enthusiasm and collective agreement.

"The crowd acclaimed her as the greatest athlete of her generation."
"He was acclaimed the winner before the official results were even announced."

Notice the structure here: acclaim + someone + as + [title/role]. The enthusiasm is still there, but the focus shifts slightly toward recognition — calling someone something, not just praising them.

Many words mean "to praise," but acclaim is special in a few ways:

It is intense. You don't acclaim something for being decent or good. Acclaim is reserved for things that are extraordinary — brilliant, exceptional, groundbreaking. A singer is acclaimed when people think they're remarkable, not just when they enjoy the music.

It is public. Acclaim almost always involves a visible, open expression of approval — audiences, critics, crowds, entire nations. A whispered compliment in private is not acclaim.

It is often shared. Acclaim frequently comes from many people together, not just one person. When something is acclaimed, there's usually a consensus of praise — a collective "yes, this is brilliant."

It often comes from a position of judgment. Critics, experts, and audiences who acclaim something are implying that they have evaluated it and found it truly worthy. This gives the word a tone of authority and significance.
Who or What Can Be Acclaimed?

Almost anything that can be evaluated and admired:

  • People — artists, athletes, leaders, scientists

"She was acclaimed as one of the finest novelists of her time."

  • Works — films, books, albums, paintings, plays

"The novel was internationally acclaimed."

  • Performances or achievements

"His speech was acclaimed across the country."

  • Concepts or decisions (less common, but possible)

"The new policy was acclaimed by human rights organizations."

• acclaimed as → "acclaimed as a genius / as the best / as a hero"
  • widely acclaimed → praised by many people across a large area
  • internationally / universally acclaimed → praised across the world or by everyone
  • critically acclaimed → praised specifically by professional critics (reviewers, experts)

"The play was widely acclaimed by audiences and critics alike."
"It was her most critically acclaimed performance."

• It is not passive. There is energy and feeling in acclaim — it's not a cold certificate of merit.
  • It is not reserved. Modest or hesitant praise is not acclaim.
  • It is not personal flattery. Telling your friend "you look great today" is not acclaiming them. Acclaim has a broader, more public quality.
  • It is not guaranteed or automatic. To be acclaimed means you earned that recognition. Acclaim is given freely by others, not claimed by yourself.
How It Feels as a Word

Acclaim carries a tone of grandeur and significance. When you say something was "acclaimed," you are signaling that it rose above the ordinary and earned the admiration of the world. It is a word that belongs in moments of genuine greatness — the kind of praise that history remembers.
179:
When something or someone is acclaimed, it means they have been publicly and enthusiastically praised by a large number of people — especially by people whose opinion carries weight, like experts, critics, or the general public at large.

Think of it this way: if you do something great, a friend might say "well done." But if critics, reviewers, experts, audiences, and the general public all come forward to say "this is exceptional, this is brilliant, this deserves recognition" — that is when you become acclaimed. It is praise that is loud, widespread, and serious.

The word "acclaimed" does not just mean liked or popular. It carries a stronger, more specific meaning. It tells you three things at once:

  1. The praise is strong — not mild or polite, but enthusiastic and heartfelt.
  2. The praise is widespread — it comes from many people, not just one or two.
  3. The praise is credible — it typically comes from people in a position to judge (critics, experts, peers in a field, or a broad and informed public).

So when you call something "acclaimed," you are signalling that the praise it has received is significant and trustworthy, not just hype.
What Kinds of Things Can Be "Acclaimed"?

Almost anything that can be judged by people can be acclaimed:

  • A person: an acclaimed author, an acclaimed scientist, an acclaimed chef
  • A creative work: an acclaimed novel, an acclaimed film, an acclaimed album
  • A performance: an acclaimed stage performance
  • A career or achievement: an acclaimed career in medicine

The word is most commonly used in the arts, entertainment, literature, and academic or professional fields — anywhere where expert opinion and public reception matter.
The Degree of Praise It Implies

"Acclaimed" sits at the high end of the praise spectrum. Compare:

  • Liked → mild positive feeling
  • Well-received → people responded positively
  • Praised → people spoke well of it
  • Highly praised → strong positive reception
  • Acclaimed → enthusiastic, widespread, and credible recognition — often approaching or at the level of greatness

It is not the absolute strongest word in English (something can be called legendary or iconic to go even further), but "acclaimed" is notably strong. Using it about something mediocre would feel like an exaggeration to most people.

You will almost always see "acclaimed" paired with words that reinforce just how strong the praise is:

  • Widely acclaimed — praised by a very large number of people
  • Critically acclaimed — praised specifically by professional critics and reviewers
  • Universally acclaimed — praised by virtually everyone; almost no one disagreed
  • Internationally acclaimed — praised across different countries and cultures

"Critically acclaimed" is perhaps the most common combination. When a film or book is called "critically acclaimed," it means professional reviewers — not just casual audiences — gave it strong, serious praise.

• The director's new film is critically acclaimed — reviewers called it one of the best of the decade.
  • She is an acclaimed novelist whose books have won several major awards.
  • The restaurant is widely acclaimed for its innovative approach to traditional cooking.
  • His acclaimed research changed the way scientists understand the human brain.

This is important to understand clearly:

  • It does not simply mean famous. Something can be famous for bad reasons (infamous, controversial). "Acclaimed" specifically means famous for being genuinely good and widely recognized as such.
  • It does not mean commercially successful. A book can sell millions of copies without being acclaimed by critics. Conversely, an acclaimed book might not always be a bestseller.
  • It does not mean loved by everyone without exception. Even "universally acclaimed" works have some detractors. The word means the dominant, overwhelming response was very positive.

When a writer chooses the word "acclaimed" over simpler words like "good" or "popular," they are making a deliberate choice to signal prestige and earned reputation. It tells the reader: this is not just my opinion — the world has looked at this and agreed it is excellent. It carries a sense of collective, validated recognition.
One-Line Summary to Remember It By
Acclaimed = widely and enthusiastically praised by many people — especially experts or critics — to the point where the person or thing is recognized as truly excellent.
180:
Acclamation is the loud, enthusiastic, collective approval or praise that a group of people expresses together — through cheering, clapping, or shouting — to show that they strongly agree with or admire something or someone.

The key ingredients are:

  • It comes from a group, not a single person.
  • It is enthusiastic and loud, not quiet or mild.
  • It is collective — people are expressing the same feeling at the same time.
  • It often implies that the agreement is widespread or unanimous (meaning everyone, or nearly everyone, agrees).

The word "acclamation" is used in two closely related situations:

1. General Use — Loud Praise or Cheering

This is the broader, everyday use. When a crowd enthusiastically cheers, claps, or shouts to show admiration or approval for someone, that expression is called acclamation.

Think of a musician finishing a concert and the entire audience jumping to their feet and roaring with cheers. That thunderous, united response from the crowd is acclamation.

Examples:

  • "The hero was welcomed home with great acclamation."
  • "The speaker's words were met with acclamation from the audience."
  • "The award-winning film received acclamation from critics and viewers alike."

Notice that in this use, acclamation is about praising or celebrating something publicly and loudly.

2. Formal Use — Elected or Decided "By Acclamation"

This is the more specific and commonly tested use of the word. It comes up in voting, elections, and official decisions.

"By acclamation" means that a decision was made or a person was chosen through open, unanimous enthusiasm — rather than through a formal, private vote where each person quietly casts a ballot.

In other words, instead of counting written votes, the group simply cheers or voices agreement together, and because the approval is so clear and strong, no formal vote is even needed.

Examples:

  • "She was elected club president by acclamation — everyone immediately agreed."
  • "The proposal was passed by acclamation at the town meeting."
  • "The retiring coach was given the honorary title by acclamation."

A helpful way to picture it: Imagine a meeting where someone suggests a popular idea. Instead of the chairperson saying "let's write down our votes," everyone just nods, cheers, and says "yes!" loudly — and the decision is made right there. That's a decision made by acclamation.
The Essential Qualities That Define Acclamation

Understanding these qualities will help you use and recognise the word correctly every time:

1. It is always collective.
One person clapping alone is not acclamation. Acclamation requires a group responding together.

2. It is enthusiastic, not passive.
Mild, polite applause doesn't qualify. Acclamation carries a sense of energy, fervour, and shared excitement. It is unmistakable.

3. It is public and open.
Acclamation is expressed outwardly — through voices, hands, and bodies. A group silently agreeing in their heads is not acclamation.

4. It often implies unanimity or near-unanimity.
When something receives acclamation, the implication is that most or all of the people present agree or approve. It's not a divided, half-hearted response — it is overwhelming agreement.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Acclamation vs. Applause:
Applause specifically means clapping. Acclamation is broader — it includes clapping, cheering, shouting, and any other vocal or physical expression of enthusiastic group approval.

Acclamation vs. Ovation:
An ovation (especially a standing ovation) is actually a type of acclamation, but "ovation" specifically refers to prolonged applause after a performance. Acclamation is the wider term that covers any enthusiastic group approval, including in voting and official contexts.

Acclamation vs. Acclaim:
These two are closely related. Acclaim (without the "-ation") is also a noun meaning praise or approval, and is used more casually (e.g., "she received great acclaim"). Acclamation is the more formal version and is the word you'll see in official, political, or ceremonial contexts — especially in the phrase "by acclamation."

These are the natural word pairings you'll encounter most often:

  • "by acclamation" — the most important phrase; means chosen or decided through unanimous enthusiasm, not a formal vote.
  • "universal acclamation" — praised or approved by absolutely everyone.
  • "receive/win acclamation" — to be praised or applauded by a group.
  • "greeted with acclamation" — welcomed enthusiastically by a crowd.
  • "popular acclamation" — approval or choice made by the general public, often used in historical or political writing.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

Acclamation is the loud, enthusiastic, collective expression of approval or agreement by a group. In everyday life, it means a crowd's cheering praise. In formal situations — like elections or official decisions — something done "by acclamation" means it was approved unanimously through open enthusiasm, with no need for a formal vote.

If you remember just one thing: acclamation is group enthusiasm made visible and audible — whether to praise someone or to approve a decision.
181:
To acclimate means to gradually get used to a new or unfamiliar condition — whether physical, environmental, or situational — until it no longer feels difficult, uncomfortable, or strange.

The key word is gradually. Acclimating is never instant. It is a process that unfolds over time, and at the end of it, something that once felt hard or foreign now feels normal.
The two ways this verb works

Acclimate can work in two directions:

1. You acclimate (yourself) to something.
Here, you are the one doing the adjusting. You are the one changing internally to match the new condition.

"She moved from sea level to a high-altitude city and needed two weeks to acclimate to the thin air."

2. You acclimate someone or something else.
Here, you are helping another person, animal, or thing go through that adjustment process.

"The wildlife team slowly acclimated the rescued eagle to outdoor conditions before releasing it."

In both cases, the core idea is the same: a gradual, internal adjustment to something new.
The preposition that goes with it

Acclimate almost always pairs with the preposition "to" — you acclimate to something.

He is acclimating to his new school.
The plants were acclimated to the colder greenhouse.
What kinds of things can a person acclimate to?

This is where the word becomes wonderfully versatile. People, animals, and even plants can acclimate to almost anything new:

Physical environments:

Soldiers acclimate to desert heat before deployment.
Mountaineers spend days at base camp to acclimate to the altitude before climbing higher.

Social or professional situations:

Starting a new job is overwhelming at first, but most people acclimate within a few weeks.
The new student was quiet at first but slowly acclimated to the social life of the school.

Cultural shifts:

After immigrating, it took her a year to fully acclimate to the customs and pace of life in her new country.

Biology and nature:

Scientists acclimated the coral samples to slightly warmer water temperatures to study their response.
Before planting seedlings outside, gardeners acclimate them by placing them outdoors for a few hours each day — a process called "hardening off."
What makes acclimating different from just "getting used to" something?

Technically, "getting used to" and "acclimating" are close cousins, but acclimate carries a stronger, more deliberate sense. It implies:

  • A meaningful or significant change in conditions (not just a minor inconvenience)
  • A real, measurable internal shift — your body, mind, or behavior actually changes
  • A process, not a single moment

You would not say "I acclimated to the traffic noise from the street." But you would say "After moving to the mountains, it took her a month to acclimate to the altitude."
How it differs from similar words

Adapt is broader. You adapt to life's challenges in general. You acclimate specifically to a new environment or condition you've been placed in.

Adjust is similar but lighter. Adjusting can be quick and minor. Acclimating is deeper — it often involves a real physiological or psychological shift.

Acclimate sits somewhere between the two — more specific than adapt, deeper than adjust.
Important nuance: the discomfort is implied

When you say someone is acclimating, it quietly implies that things were difficult before and will become easier after. The word carries a built-in story arc: struggle → adjustment → normalcy.

If someone was never uncomfortable to begin with, you wouldn't use this word. Saying "she acclimated to the pleasant weather" sounds odd, because there was no challenge to overcome.

All of these come from the same root and you'll see them often:

  • Acclimating — present tense, the process is ongoing → "He is still acclimating to the night shifts."
  • Acclimated — past tense, or used as an adjective → "After a month, she was fully acclimated."
  • Acclimation — the noun form, referring to the process or the state → "Acclimation to high altitude can take days."
  • Acclimatize — an alternate verb form with the exact same meaning, more common in British English → "The team needed time to acclimatize."
  • Acclimatization — the noun form of acclimatize, again same meaning as acclimation.
One sentence to remember it by
To acclimate is to slowly become comfortable with something new and demanding — to let your body, mind, or behavior quietly reshape itself until the unfamiliar becomes familiar.
182:
To acclimatize means to gradually get used to something new — a new place, a new environment, a new situation, or new conditions — so that it starts to feel normal and manageable.

The key word here is gradually. Acclimatizing is never instant. It is a process that takes time.
The Two Ways It Is Used

1. The Literal (Physical) Meaning

This is the original, most precise meaning. When your body physically adjusts to a new climate or environment — especially one that is challenging — that is acclimatizing.

Think of a person who lives at sea level and then travels to a mountain that is 4,000 metres high. The air up there is thin, with less oxygen. At first, they feel breathless, dizzy, and tired. But over several days, their body starts producing more red blood cells, their breathing becomes more efficient, and they feel better. Their body has acclimatized to the altitude.

This happens in other physical situations too:

  • A person from a cold country moving to a hot, humid country — their body acclimatizes to the heat over weeks.
  • A deep-sea diver whose body acclimatizes to the pressure gradually.
  • A person starting to exercise regularly — their lungs and muscles acclimatize to the physical demand.

The body is doing real, biological work during this process. It is not just a feeling — it is a measurable physical change.

2. The Figurative (Mental/Emotional) Meaning

This is the extended, everyday meaning of the word. Here, it is not your body that adjusts — it is your mind, emotions, and behaviour.

When you face a new situation that feels unfamiliar, strange, or uncomfortable, and you slowly begin to feel at ease with it, you are acclimatizing.

Examples:

  • A student from India who moves to Canada for university. Everything is new — the culture, the food, the social customs, the weather, the pace of life. In the first weeks, they feel lost. But over months, they slowly understand how things work, they make friends, they stop feeling like an outsider. They have acclimatized to life in Canada.
  • A person who starts a new job. The environment, the people, the systems, the expectations — all unfamiliar. After a few weeks, they begin to feel more comfortable and confident. They are acclimatizing to the workplace.
  • Someone who grew up in a quiet village and moves to a loud, fast-paced city. Initially, the noise and crowd feel overwhelming. Gradually, it starts feeling normal. They have acclimatized to city life.
How the Word Works in a Sentence

"Acclimatize" is flexible. It can be used in three patterns:

Pattern 1 — The subject adjusts on their own:

"She slowly acclimatized to the cold winters."
"It took him a month to acclimatize to night shifts."

Pattern 2 — Something or someone helps another person adjust (transitive use):

"The training programme was designed to acclimatize new soldiers to extreme conditions."
"The orientation week helped acclimatize the students to university life."

Pattern 3 — The subject consciously adjusts themselves (reflexive use):

"He had to acclimatize himself to a completely different way of working."
"She acclimatized herself to the idea of living alone."
An Important Nuance: It Always Implies a Challenge

You would not say someone acclimatized to eating their favourite food or sleeping in a comfortable bed. The word carries a subtle implication that the new thing was difficult, unfamiliar, or demanding at first. There is always some initial resistance — physical or emotional — that the person (or animal) has to overcome.

This makes it a stronger and more specific word than just saying "got used to." It suggests a real process of adjustment in the face of something that was not easy.
It Can Be Used for Animals Too

It is not just for humans. Animals can acclimatize as well:

"The zoo took several weeks to acclimatize the polar bear to the warmer climate."
"Fish need time to acclimatize when introduced to a new tank."

The noun form — which you will often see — is acclimatization:

"Acclimatization to high altitude can take several days."
"Her acclimatization to the new culture was slow but steady."

You may also see the spelling acclimatise (with an s instead of a z). This is simply the British English spelling. Both mean exactly the same thing. Acclimatize is preferred in American English; acclimatise is preferred in British English.

Whether used literally (your body adapting to a new climate or physical condition) or figuratively (your mind and habits adjusting to a new situation), to acclimatize always means the same thing at its heart:

To go through a gradual process of adjustment until something that was once difficult, foreign, or uncomfortable becomes manageable and familiar.

It is a word about resilience, patience, and the quiet power of adaptation.
183:
An acclivity is an upward slope — the rising face of a hill, a mountain, or any piece of ground that goes up. It is the inclined surface you see and feel beneath your feet as you climb.

Imagine you're standing at the base of a hill, looking up at it. That rising, slanting surface stretching upward in front of you — that is the acclivity. The moment you start walking up it, you are walking up the acclivity.

The word is very specific: it only ever means an upward slope, never a flat surface and never a downward one. This is its sharpest quality. An acclivity has a clear direction — it always goes up.

It has a natural twin and opposite: declivity, which is a downward slope. Together, they describe the two sides of a hill — the acclivity is the side going up, and the declivity is the side coming down. A complete hill, therefore, has both: you climb the acclivity on one side and descend the declivity on the other.
It Describes Both the Surface and Its Steepness

"Acclivity" can describe two closely related things:

  1. The physical slope itself — the actual surface of ground that rises upward.
  2. The degree of the rise — how steep or gentle that upward slope is.

So you might say "a steep acclivity" (meaning a sharply rising slope, almost wall-like) or "a gentle acclivity" (meaning a soft, gradual rise, barely noticeable). The word itself doesn't fix a specific angle — it simply names the upward-slanting surface, whatever its steepness happens to be.

Acclivity is a formal and literary word. You won't hear it in everyday conversation — no one at the grocery store will say, "I jogged up a lovely acclivity this morning." Instead, you'll find it in:

  • Classic literature and 19th-century prose, where writers favoured precise, elevated language to describe landscapes.
  • Geography and natural science writing, when authors describe terrain with technical accuracy.
  • Military writing, since understanding the slope of terrain (who climbs up, who fires down) was critical in historical battle strategy.

In modern writing, it appears when an author wants to sound formal, precise, or deliberately old-fashioned.

These will show you the word working naturally in context:

  • "The weary soldiers pressed forward up the rocky acclivity, shields raised against the arrows falling from above."
  • "A long, gentle acclivity led from the valley floor toward the castle gates."
  • "The horse slowed noticeably as the road shifted from flat ground to a sharp acclivity."
  • "She paused halfway up the acclivity, breathing hard, the village now small and distant below her."

If you ever want to remember it instantly:

Acclivity = the side of a slope going up.

Think of the phrase "climbing a hill" — the hill's surface climbing upward beneath you is the acclivity. And if you ever mix it up with "declivity," just remember: de- means down (like descend), and ac- here pulls you upward.

To keep the definition sharp:

  • It is not a flat road or surface.
  • It is not a downward slope (that's a declivity).
  • It is not a cliff or vertical face — an acclivity is an inclined slope, not a sheer drop or wall.
  • It is not the hill as a whole — only the rising face of it.
An acclivity is the upward-slanting face of a slope — the rising surface of terrain as it ascends — and it is the formal, precise opposite of a downward slope (called a declivity).
184:
An accolade is a recognition of excellence given to someone by others. It is a way of saying, publicly or formally: "What you did was outstanding, and we want to acknowledge it."

Think of it as a stamp of approval from the world — earned, not given freely.

An accolade can be one of two closely related things:

1. A concrete award, prize, or honor
This is when an organization or institution formally recognizes someone's achievement with something tangible or official — a trophy, a title, a certificate, a nomination. The Oscar statuette is an accolade. A Nobel Prize is an accolade. Being named "Employee of the Year" is an accolade.

2. Strong, meaningful praise
This is when people — critics, peers, the public, experts — express very high admiration for someone's work or achievement. No physical prize is involved, but the recognition is still real and significant. When every film critic in the country praises a director's new movie as a masterpiece, those glowing reviews are accolades too.

The common thread in both cases: an accolade always comes from outside yourself. You cannot give yourself an accolade. It must come from others, and it must be in recognition of something genuinely impressive.
What Makes Something an Accolade (and Not Just a Compliment)?

This is an important distinction. Not every kind word is an accolade.

Your friend telling you, "Hey, nice haircut!" is a compliment — small, casual, personal.

But when a respected institution, a panel of experts, or a wide group of people single you out and say your work is exceptional? That is an accolade. The word carries weight and prestige. It implies that the recognition is:

  • Earned through real merit or achievement
  • Meaningful, coming from a source that matters
  • Noteworthy enough to be worth mentioning

So the word sits above ordinary praise on the scale of recognition.

Accolades exist on a spectrum:

At the most formal end, you have actual awards with ceremonies — think Grammy Awards, Olympic gold medals, Pulitzer Prizes, knighthoods. These are undeniably accolades.

Moving along the spectrum, you have things like a five-star review from a prestigious publication, being praised by a legendary figure in your field, or receiving a standing ovation — no trophy, but still a powerful form of recognition. These are also accolades.
