At the less formal end, the word can describe a collection of strong, positive responses to someone's work — like saying an author "received accolades from readers worldwide." Here it means widespread admiration and approval.

In all cases, the core idea holds: something worthy was done, and the world took notice and said so.

In a more specific, traditional context — particularly in history and formal ceremonies — an accolade refers to the ceremonial act of conferring knighthood. In medieval times, a king or queen would physically touch a sword to a person's shoulders to officially make them a knight. That moment of conferral was called the accolade.

Even today, this meaning survives in formal settings. When the British monarch taps a person on the shoulders with a sword during an investiture ceremony, that gesture is the accolade. In this sense, the word refers to the specific act of bestowing an honor, not just the honor itself.

Here are examples that cover the full range of meaning:

  • "The surgeon received the highest accolade in her field when she was awarded the Lasker Prize." (a formal award)
  • "The novel earned widespread critical accolades upon its release." (strong praise from critics)
  • "For an athlete, representing their country at the Olympics is the ultimate accolade." (the greatest form of recognition)
  • "Despite the film's box office failure, it gathered surprising accolades from independent reviewers." (positive recognition from a specific group)
  • "She has received numerous accolades throughout her career." (a general accumulation of honors and recognitions)

Notice that "accolades" is very frequently used in the plural — because recognition often comes in many forms and from many directions at once.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what the word does not mean:

  • It is not criticism, even constructive criticism. An accolade is always positive.
  • It is not self-praise. You receive accolades; you do not give them to yourself.
  • It is not routine acknowledgment. Being thanked for doing your job is not an accolade. Being honored as the best in your field is.
  • It is not flattery. Flattery is insincere and often exaggerated. An accolade implies genuine merit behind the recognition.

To put it simply: an accolade is a meaningful, merit-based recognition of excellence, given by others. It can be a formal award or powerful praise, but it always signals that someone has achieved something genuinely impressive and that the world has acknowledged it. The word carries a sense of prestige and significance — it is not thrown around lightly, and when you use it or hear it, it tells you that something (or someone) truly stood out.
185: At the heart of every meaning of "accommodate" is one simple idea: adjusting or making room so that something or someone fits comfortably. That "room" can be physical space, a set of rules, a plan, or even your own attitude. The word always involves some kind of stretching or bending to make a fit happen.

1. To provide physical space for people or things

When a place accommodates a number of people or things, it means it has enough space to hold or contain them comfortably.

"The new stadium accommodates 80,000 fans."
"The hotel can accommodate up to 300 guests."
"This suitcase is big enough to accommodate all your clothes."

Notice that the subject is always a place or container. You're describing its capacity — what it can physically hold.

2. To adjust or make special arrangements to meet someone's needs

This is the most common and important meaning in everyday life. To accommodate someone here means to willingly change, adjust, or rearrange things so that a particular person's needs, wishes, or situation are taken care of.

"The school accommodated students with disabilities by providing ramps and special seating."
"The chef accommodated our vegetarian requests."
"Can the airline accommodate passengers with severe nut allergies?"
"We will do our best to accommodate your request."

The key feeling here is flexibility and consideration. The person or organization is going out of their way to make sure you are not left out, disadvantaged, or uncomfortable. It is an act of care.

3. To adapt yourself to a new situation

Here, instead of adjusting things for someone else, you are the one doing the adjusting — fitting yourself into a new environment, situation, or reality.

"It took her a few weeks to accommodate herself to life in a new country."
"New employees are expected to accommodate to the company's culture."

Think of it as: you are the one doing the stretching, not for another person's benefit, but to fit into your new surroundings.

4. To do someone a favor or oblige them

In a more formal or old-fashioned sense, to accommodate someone means to help them out or do them a kindness. This sense is less common in modern everyday English, but you'll still come across it in formal writing.

"The bank accommodated him with a loan."
"She accommodated her neighbor by looking after his dog."
The Thread That Connects All Four Meanings

Every single meaning of "accommodate" comes back to the same invisible thread: making something fit by adjusting.

A stadium fits people in physically. A school fits its rules around a student's special needs. A person fits themselves into a new culture. A bank fits a customer's financial need. The what changes across the meanings, but the act of adjusting to create a fit is always there.

"Accommodate" always carries a sense of willingness and effort. When someone accommodates you, they are choosing to be flexible — often going slightly out of their way. It's never forced or reluctant. This is why the word has a naturally generous, considerate tone. "The restaurant accommodated our last-minute change" quietly implies that it wasn't entirely easy, but they did it anyway.

The word is also quite formal. It belongs naturally in professional emails, hotel notices, business conversations, and official documents. In casual speech, people often swap it for simpler phrases:

Instead of "We will accommodate your request," someone might say: "We'll make it work."
Instead of "She accommodated herself to the new city," someone might say: "She got used to the new city."

Knowing this helps you understand when to use "accommodate" — lean toward it in formal, professional, or polished contexts.

These are the most natural combinations in real English:

accommodate a request — to agree to and fulfill a request
accommodate a need / requirement — to make arrangements to meet a specific need
accommodate guests / visitors — to provide space and comfort for people
accommodate differences — to accept and make room for variations between people
accommodate change — to adapt to changes
accommodate up to [number] — to have capacity for a certain number of people or things
How It Compares to Similar Words

"Adjust" is more neutral — it just means to change something. "Accommodate" adds the layer of doing it for someone's benefit.

"Hold" or "fit" (as in physical capacity) are purely about size. "The bus holds 40 people" is flat and mechanical. "The bus accommodates 40 people" suggests it does so comfortably and purposefully.

"Adapt" usually means you are changing yourself to deal with a broad or ongoing situation. "Accommodate" is more targeted — you are changing for a specific person, need, or request.

To accommodate means to adjust, make room, or arrange things so that a person or need fits comfortably. It can describe a place having space (a hotel that accommodates 200 guests), an organization being flexible (a school that accommodates disabled students), a person adapting themselves (she accommodated herself to the new culture), or someone doing a favor (the bank accommodated him). Across all its uses, the word implies willingness, flexibility, and a degree of effort — and it lives most naturally in formal, professional language.
186:
Accommodating describes a person who is willing to adjust themselves — their plans, preferences, or behavior — to fit the needs or wishes of others. An accommodating person makes life easier for the people around them by being flexible, cooperative, and helpful.

Think of it this way: imagine you have a friend who, without much fuss, always finds a way to work around your needs. You're running late? They wait patiently. You have a food allergy? They pick a restaurant that suits you. You need a favor? They say yes without making it a big deal. That friend is accommodating.
What It Actually Means to Be Accommodating

An accommodating person has two key qualities working together:

Willingness — they want to help or adjust. They don't feel forced. They genuinely don't mind bending to suit others.

Flexibility — they can adjust. They don't rigidly stick to their own way of doing things when someone else has a different need.

Both qualities must be present. Someone who wants to help but can't change anything isn't accommodating. Someone who can change but refuses to isn't accommodating either. The word lives in the overlap of both.

"Accommodating" almost always describes people, but it can also describe organizations, policies, systems, or environments.

People: a teacher, a hotel receptionist, a boss, a colleague, a landlord.

Things: a company policy, a schedule, a system.

The word describes a personality trait or a behavior, not a one-time act. Saying someone is accommodating suggests it is a consistent pattern in how they deal with people, not just something they did once.

These examples will show you the word at work in real situations:

  • "Our landlord is very accommodating — when we asked if we could paint the walls, he agreed without any hesitation."
  • "The hotel staff were incredibly accommodating and moved us to a quieter room as soon as we asked."
  • "She's always so accommodating that she rarely says no to anyone."
  • "The school has an accommodating policy that allows students to reschedule exams if they're ill."
  • "He's easy to work with because he's calm and accommodating, even when plans change last minute."

Notice how in each case, someone (or something) is bending, adjusting, or going the extra mile for another person's comfort or convenience.
The Tone of the Word — Is It Positive or Negative?

In most situations, "accommodating" is a compliment. It suggests someone is pleasant, cooperative, and considerate. If a manager describes you as accommodating, it's generally a good thing — it means you're easy to work with and you care about others' needs.

However, the word can carry a mildly negative shade depending on context. If someone is too accommodating, it can imply they are a pushover — that they agree to everything, never stand up for themselves, and can be taken advantage of easily. You'll usually see this expressed with words like "overly," "too," or "excessively":

  • "He's so accommodating that people take advantage of him."
  • "She was too accommodating and ended up doing everyone else's work."

So the word sits on a spectrum: being accommodating is a virtue, but being excessively accommodating can become a weakness.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning, but each has a slightly different flavor:

Helpful is broader — it just means willing to assist. An accommodating person is helpful, but "accommodating" specifically emphasizes adjusting to fit someone else, not just helping in general.

Flexible focuses on the ability to change plans or attitudes. An accommodating person is flexible, but "accommodating" adds a social warmth to it — it implies doing so for the sake of others.

Obliging means willing to do what is asked. It's nearly synonymous with accommodating, but slightly more formal and less commonly used in everyday conversation.

Easygoing means relaxed and not easily bothered. An easygoing person tends to be accommodating, but easygoing is about their attitude, while accommodating is about their actions toward others.

Cooperative means willing to work with others toward a shared goal. It's close, but cooperative focuses on teamwork, while accommodating focuses on putting others' needs first.

Synonyms (words with a similar meaning): helpful, obliging, flexible, cooperative, considerate, easygoing, willing, agreeable.

Antonyms (words with the opposite meaning): unaccommodating, rigid, inflexible, unhelpful, difficult, demanding, uncooperative.

If you want to remember this word in one line:

An accommodating person is someone who willingly adjusts themselves to make things easier or more comfortable for others.

That's the beating heart of the word. Everything else — the nuance, the context, the degree — grows from that single idea.
187:
Before looking at individual meanings, here is the single idea that runs through all of them: making room or making adjustments so that something or someone can fit comfortably.

Whether it is a physical space, a rule, a plan, or even your eye — "accommodation" always involves adjusting or providing something so that a need is met. Keep this in mind as you read through the meanings below.

This is the most common, everyday meaning. An accommodation is a place where a person can sleep, live, or stay — especially on a temporary basis. Hotels, guesthouses, hostels, rented rooms, and furnished apartments are all examples of accommodation.

Examples:

  • "We booked accommodation near the airport."
  • "The university provides accommodation for first-year students."
  • "Finding affordable accommodation in the city was difficult."

Important note on grammar:
In British English (used in India, the UK, Australia, etc.), this meaning is almost always used as an uncountable noun — meaning you do not add "s" and you do not say "an accommodation" when referring to a place to stay. You say "accommodation" (without "an" or "s").

  • ✅ "We need accommodation."
  • ❌ "We need an accommodation." (in the British sense)

In American English, people commonly say "accommodations" (plural) to mean a place to stay, especially in travel contexts.

  • ✅ "The hotel accommodations were excellent." (American)

Both are correct in their respective varieties of English — just know which one you are using.
Meaning 2: A Compromise or Mutual Agreement

When two people or groups have different needs or wants, and they adjust their positions to reach a middle ground that works for everyone, that agreement or compromise is called an accommodation.

This meaning captures the idea of give and take — one or both sides bending a little so that both can move forward together.

Examples:

  • "After weeks of disagreement, the two companies finally reached an accommodation."
  • "The new policy was an accommodation between the workers' demands and the management's budget."
  • "They came to an accommodation about how to share the space."

Think of it like two people trying to sit on a narrow bench — each shifts a little to make room for the other. That act of shifting and fitting together is the accommodation.
Meaning 3: A Special Adjustment Made for Someone's Needs

This is one of the most important and widely used meanings in formal, legal, educational, and workplace contexts.

An accommodation (usually used in the plural: accommodations) refers to a specific adjustment, change, or special arrangement made to help someone — particularly a person with a disability, a medical condition, or a special need — participate equally and fairly.

The logic here is: if the standard rules or environment create an unfair barrier for someone, you change or adjust them to remove that barrier. That change is the accommodation.

Examples:

  • "The school provided accommodations for students with dyslexia, such as extra time during exams and the option to use a computer."
  • "The company offered workplace accommodations to an employee recovering from surgery, including a flexible work schedule."
  • "Requesting accommodations is your right as a student with a disability."

This meaning is especially common in education and employment law. The key idea is fairness through adjustment — the accommodation does not give someone an unfair advantage; it removes an unfair disadvantage.
Meaning 4: The General Act of Adapting or Adjusting

More broadly, "accommodation" can refer to the process of adapting yourself — or something — to fit a situation, a new reality, or someone else's requirements. This is a slightly more abstract and formal use.

Examples:

  • "The accommodation of so many different cultural traditions within one curriculum is a real challenge."
  • "His quick accommodation to the new environment surprised everyone."
  • "The law requires reasonable accommodation of employees' religious practices."

Here, the word essentially means the act of fitting in, adjusting, or making space for something.
Meaning 5: In Biology — How the Eye Focuses

This is a technical, scientific meaning used in biology and medicine.

Accommodation refers to the automatic ability of the eye to adjust its focus when looking at objects at different distances. When you shift your gaze from a book in your hand to a tree far away, your eye's lens changes shape to keep the image clear. That automatic change in the lens is called accommodation.

Example:

  • "With age, the eye's ability for accommodation decreases, which is why many older people need reading glasses."
Meaning 6: In Psychology — How the Mind Adjusts to New Information

This meaning comes from the developmental psychologist Jean Piaget, and it is widely used in education and psychology.

Piaget described two processes by which people learn and make sense of the world:

  • Assimilation — fitting new information into a mental framework you already have. For example, a child who knows "dogs" might call a cat a "dog" because it fits their existing idea.
  • Accommodation — changing your existing mental framework because new information does not fit into it. For example, when the child learns that cats are different from dogs, they adjust their mental categories. That adjustment is accommodation.

So in psychology, accommodation is the process of updating or restructuring your understanding to make room for something new that your old understanding could not explain.

Examples:

  • "When the child encountered a whale for the first time, accommodation occurred — she had to revise her understanding of what an 'animal' is."
  • "Learning that the Earth is round, not flat, requires accommodation of prior mental schemas."

Every meaning of "accommodation" flows from the same core idea — making room, adjusting, or fitting something in:

  • A hotel room makes physical room for you to stay.
  • A compromise makes relational room for two different positions to coexist.
  • A special adjustment makes practical room for a person with a different need to participate equally.
  • Adapting to a situation is making room in your life or plans for new realities.
  • The eye makes optical room by adjusting its lens to focus.
  • The mind makes cognitive room by updating its understanding to fit new information.
A Subtle but Important Quality of the Word

"Accommodation" almost always implies goodwill and cooperation. When someone makes an accommodation for you, they are being helpful, flexible, and considerate. It is not a reluctant, forced act — it carries the tone of willingness to adjust for someone else's benefit.

This is why the word appears so often in polite, professional, and legal language. Saying "we will make accommodations" sounds generous and respectful; it signals that someone's needs have been genuinely heard and will be met.

• When the meaning is a place to stay, use it as an uncountable noun in standard (British-style) English: "We need accommodation."
  • When the meaning is special adjustments made for someone's needs, it is almost always plural: "The school provided accommodations."
  • When the meaning is a compromise or agreement, it is often used with "an" or "reach": "They reached an accommodation."
188:
Accompaniment means something that goes along with something else — something that exists alongside a main thing, usually in a supporting or complementary role. The key idea baked into this word is pairing: one thing is primary (the main focus), and the accompaniment is the secondary thing that travels with it, supports it, or happens at the same time as it.

Think of it this way: an accompaniment is never the star. It exists because of the star, and its job is to make the star shine better, feel more complete, or simply coexist naturally alongside it.

This word is used meaningfully in three different contexts. Understanding all three will give you complete command of the word.

1. In Music (the most specific sense)

This is where the word is used most precisely. In music, accompaniment refers to the background music that supports a lead performer — a singer, a violinist, a flutist, or any soloist. The accompaniment is not the melody you pay attention to; it is the harmonic and rhythmic support underneath that melody that makes it sound full, rich, and complete.

For example:

  • A pianist playing flowing chords while a singer performs a song — the piano part is the accompaniment.
  • An orchestra playing behind a solo violinist — the orchestra is providing accompaniment.
  • A guitarist strumming chords while someone else sings — the guitar is the accompaniment.

The accompaniment and the lead performer work together, but they are not equal in focus. The accompaniment is in service of the main performer. If you removed it, the performance would feel thin or bare. If you removed the main performer, the accompaniment alone would feel incomplete and purposeless.

A person who plays accompaniment is called an accompanist.

2. In Food (a culinary sense)

In cooking and dining, an accompaniment is a food item served alongside a main dish to complement it — to enhance the eating experience, add balance, or simply round out the meal.

For example:

  • Bread served with a bowl of soup — the bread is the accompaniment.
  • A mint sauce served alongside roast lamb — the mint sauce is the accompaniment.
  • A side salad, roasted vegetables, or mashed potatoes served with a steak — these are all accompaniments.

Notice again the same logic: the steak is the main dish, and the sides exist to support and complement it. They are not afterthoughts — they genuinely improve the experience — but they are not the centerpiece either.

3. In General / Everyday Use (a broader, figurative sense)

Outside music and food, accompaniment is used more broadly to describe anything that happens at the same time as something else, or that naturally and regularly goes together with something else. In this sense, it often describes two things that are so naturally linked that one seems to bring the other along with it.

For example:

  • "She fell asleep to the accompaniment of rain pattering on the roof."
    Here, the rain is happening at the same time as she is falling asleep, and it is setting the background atmosphere, much like music does.
  • "The announcement was made to the accompaniment of loud applause."
    The applause happened simultaneously with the announcement, creating the backdrop for it.
  • "Anxiety is a common accompaniment of major life changes."
    This means anxiety tends to come along with big life changes — it regularly pairs with them.

In this general sense, the accompaniment is anything that is a natural partner, a background presence, or a simultaneous occurrence to something else.
The One Big Idea That Ties It All Together

No matter which context you see "accompaniment" in — music, food, or everyday life — the same logic always applies:

There is a primary thing, and there is the accompaniment. The accompaniment exists alongside the primary thing, in a supporting or complementary role. It adds to it, enriches it, or simply travels with it. But it is not the main focus.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Seeing a word in different sentences makes it stick far better, so here are several natural examples across all senses:

  • "The pianist provided a beautiful accompaniment to the soprano's singing." (music)
  • "Roasted potatoes make an excellent accompaniment to grilled chicken." (food)
  • "He spoke quietly, his words barely audible above the accompaniment of traffic noise outside." (general)
  • "Laughter is a welcome accompaniment to any good meal." (general/figurative)
  • "The choir sang without any musical accompaniment — just their voices, nothing else." (music — notable because here the absence of accompaniment is being pointed out)
  • "Stress is often an unwelcome accompaniment of ambition." (general/figurative)

The word carries a subtle sense of naturalness or fittingness in the pairing. An accompaniment is not just anything randomly placed next to something else — it is something that belongs there, that feels right alongside the main thing, whether because it was designed that way (a pianist hired for a concert), or because it happens so often that the two things feel naturally linked (anxiety and big change).

This is why "accompaniment" sounds more refined and intentional than simply saying "something that was also there."

SenseWhat it meansExample

In music, it's the supporting background music for a main performer. In food, it's a side dish or condiment that goes with the main course. In general use, it's anything that naturally happens alongside, or pairs with, something else. In all cases, it is the secondary, supporting presence — not the star, but essential to the full picture.
189: Accompany means to go with, exist with, or occur alongside something or someone. The central image is always "together" — one thing moving or existing in parallel with another. It is never about going instead of something or before it, but always alongside it.

1. To go somewhere with a person

This is the most common meaning. When you accompany someone, you travel or go to a place together with them — usually because they need your company, support, or presence.

A nurse accompanied the patient to the operating room. His mother accompanied him on his first day of school. She asked a friend to accompany her to the interview.

The person who accompanies is usually in a supporting role. They are not leading the other person — they are simply there with them. There is a quiet warmth in this word: it suggests loyalty, care, and presence.

2. To happen or exist at the same time as something else

Not just people — events, conditions, and things can "accompany" each other too. This means they occur together, one alongside the other.

High fever often accompanies the flu. A sharp rise in prices accompanied the shortage of fuel. His promotion was accompanied by a significant increase in responsibility.

Notice something important: accompany here does not mean one thing caused the other. It simply tells you that when X happens, Y tends to come along with it — they appear as a pair or package.

3. In music, to play a supporting part while someone else performs

In a musical setting, to accompany someone means to play a background or supporting instrument — usually a piano or guitar — while a singer or solo musician performs. The one who accompanies is called the accompanist, and their role is to support the main performer, not to take the spotlight.

The pianist accompanied the soprano as she sang the final aria. He accompanied her on the guitar while she performed the folk song.

This is the most important nuance of the word, and it applies across all three meanings. A shadow accompanies a person — it is always with them, never ahead of them or separate from them. Similarly, when you accompany someone to a hospital, you are not going for them — you are going with them. When fever accompanies an illness, the fever doesn't replace the illness — both exist at the same time.

Another way to feel this: accompany carries a sense of completeness. A good wine accompanies a fine meal — it completes the experience, makes it whole. This is why the word appears so naturally in elegant, formal, or meaningful contexts.

There are two main structures to know.

Active: Subject + accompany + object. "She accompanied him to the courthouse." The subject is the one doing the accompanying.

Passive — be accompanied by: This pattern is extremely common, especially in formal writing and journalism. "The president was accompanied by his security team." / "The new policy was accompanied by a public announcement." Here, the focus shifts to the person or thing being accompanied, and the "who" or "what" comes after by.

Both patterns are equally important to recognize and use.
Register — How Formal Is This Word?

Accompany is a formal or semi-formal word. In everyday casual speech, people usually say "go with" or "come with" instead.

Casual: "Can you come with me to the dentist?"
Formal: "Will you accompany me to the appointment?"

They mean exactly the same thing. Accompany simply sounds more polished and dignified, which is why you will encounter it in newspapers, literature, official letters, professional emails, and formal speech — far more than in everyday conversation.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Follow means to go behind someone, after them. Accompany means to go beside them, together.

Lead / escort means to guide someone by going ahead of them. Accompany does not imply you are guiding — you are simply present alongside.

Attend means to be present at an event. Accompany means to be present with a specific person at that event. Attending is about being somewhere; accompanying is about being there with someone.

Whenever you see or hear accompany, ask yourself: what is traveling with what? What is existing alongside what? Whether it is a nurse walking with a patient, a fever appearing with a cold, or a piano supporting a singer — the answer will always involve two things moving through the same moment, side by side. That parallel presence, that sense of "together," is the soul of this word.
190: An accomplice is a person who helps someone else do something wrong or illegal — not the main person committing the act, but someone who plays a supporting role in it. Think of it this way: if a crime or wrongdoing is a team effort, the accomplice is not the star player, but they are very much part of the team.

For someone to truly be an accomplice, two things must be true at the same time:

1. They must help.
The help can look many different ways — driving someone to the scene of a crime, acting as a lookout, providing a weapon, sharing information, creating a distraction, or even just offering encouragement and a plan. The help doesn't have to be physical. Words, advice, and planning count too.

2. They must know what they are helping with.
This is the most important and most misunderstood part of the word. An accomplice is not someone who was tricked or kept in the dark. They knowingly assisted. If your friend asks you to drive them somewhere and you later find out they robbed a store there — without you knowing beforehand — you are not their accomplice. You were deceived. But if your friend told you exactly what they were going to do and you drove them there anyway, you are their accomplice, even if you never stepped foot inside the store.

Knowledge of the wrongdoing, combined with a choice to help anyway, is what makes someone an accomplice. Remove either one, and the label doesn't apply.

It helps to draw clear lines:

  • An innocent bystander who simply witnesses something wrong is not an accomplice. Watching is not helping.
  • A person who was forced or threatened into helping is generally not considered a true accomplice, because their "help" wasn't a free choice.
  • A person who helped without knowing anything wrong was happening is not an accomplice — they are an unknowing tool, not a willing participant.
  • The main person who actually commits the crime is called the perpetrator or the principal, not the accomplice. The accomplice supports; the perpetrator leads or executes.
The Size of the Role Doesn't Matter

One of the most important things to understand is that an accomplice's role can be enormous or tiny — and they are still an accomplice either way.

Imagine three people plan a theft. One breaks into the building, one stands outside as a lookout, and one simply lent them the tools they needed and stayed home. All three are accomplices to each other (though the law may treat their individual responsibility differently). The person at home who lent the tools played the smallest role, but they knowingly contributed to the crime. That is enough.
The Weight of Being an Accomplice

In the legal world, being an accomplice is serious. The law in most countries holds that a person who knowingly helps commit a crime shares in the guilt of that crime. This means an accomplice can be arrested, charged, and punished — sometimes just as severely as the person who actually "did the deed." The logic is straightforward: without the accomplice's help, the crime may not have happened at all. Their assistance made them morally and legally responsible.

This is why the word carries such a strong negative weight. Calling someone an accomplice is not a neutral description. It is an accusation of deliberate involvement in wrongdoing.

Outside of courts and crime, people use "accomplice" in a looser, sometimes even playful way to describe someone who helped with something mischievous, naughty, or rule-bending — but not necessarily illegal.

For example:

  • "My little brother was my accomplice in sneaking cookies from the kitchen before dinner."
  • "She was my accomplice in convincing the boss to let us leave early on Friday."

In these cases, the word is used with a light or humorous tone. The "wrongdoing" is minor and no one is going to jail. But notice the core idea still holds: someone helped someone else do something they probably shouldn't have, and they did so knowingly.
Rich Examples to Lock It In

Example 1 — Classic crime:
A man plans to rob a jewelry store. His girlfriend knows about the plan. On the day of the robbery, she creates a distraction by pretending to faint outside the store so the security guard rushes out. The man steals the jewels and escapes. She never touched a single piece of jewelry, but she is absolutely his accomplice. She knew the plan and she helped execute it.

Example 2 — No knowledge, no accomplice:
A taxi driver picks up a passenger and drives them to an address. Unknown to the driver, the passenger intends to commit fraud there. The driver is not an accomplice. They had no knowledge of any wrongdoing. They simply did their job.

Example 3 — School cheating:
During an exam, one student whispers answers to their friend. The friend who receives the answers is cheating. The student who whispers them is their accomplice in cheating. Both are guilty, just in different roles.

Example 4 — Planning without showing up:
A hacker helps a criminal gang by writing a piece of software that breaks into a bank's computer system. The hacker never visits the bank, never meets the gang in person, and sits at home the whole time. But they knowingly built the tool that made the crime possible. They are an accomplice.
How It Differs from a Similar Word: "Accessory"

You may sometimes encounter the word accessory used in a similar way, especially in legal contexts. In everyday English, the two words are often used interchangeably. In strict legal language, however, some systems make a distinction: an "accessory after the fact" is someone who helps after the crime is already done — for example, by hiding the criminal, destroying evidence, or lying to the police to protect them. An accomplice, more precisely, helps before or during the crime. But in common everyday use, don't worry too much about this distinction — both words point to someone who is knowingly involved in another person's wrongdoing.
An accomplice is someone who knowingly helps another person do something wrong — sharing in the guilt of that wrongdoing, no matter how big or small their contribution was.
191:
To accomplish something means to successfully carry a task, goal, or objective all the way through to its completion — through intent and effort.

When you accomplish something, three things are true:

A goal or task exists (something you set out to do), effort is made toward it (it doesn't happen by accident), and it is completed successfully (you reach the intended end).

All three ideas live inside this single word. That is what makes it precise and powerful.

The heart of "accomplish" is completion. Not starting. Not trying. Not being halfway there. Finishing, and finishing successfully.

This is why we say things like:

  • "She accomplished her goal of finishing college." → She set the goal, worked through it, and completed it.
  • "We accomplished the mission." → The mission is done — carried through to success.
  • "I accomplished nothing today." → No task, no goal — nothing was brought to completion.

The moment you use this word, the listener understands: it's done, and it was done on purpose.
What Kinds of Things Can Be "Accomplished"?

The word "accomplish" almost always pairs with a goal, task, objective, mission, feat, or purpose — things that have a clear intended outcome:

  • accomplish a goal
  • accomplish a task
  • accomplish a mission
  • accomplish an objective
  • accomplish a feat (something impressive or difficult)
  • accomplish nothing / little / a great deal
  • accomplish something (general)

You can also use it in questions: "What did you accomplish today?"

Importantly, the thing being accomplished must be intentional. You wouldn't say "I accomplished a headache" or "I accidentally accomplished a mess" — because those aren't purposeful goals. For unintentional results, you'd say "I caused" or "I ended up with."

"Accomplish" has a positive, purposeful tone. It implies that something meaningful was done — something that took real effort and intention. This is why it sounds strange when paired with trivial or effortless things:

  • "I finished eating." → Natural. Eating doesn't require a serious goal.
  • "I accomplished eating." → Strange. Eating is not the kind of purposeful objective this word is meant for.

Reserve "accomplish" for tasks and goals that actually carry weight — things with substance, stakes, or significance.

Several words look and feel similar to "accomplish." Each has its own shade of meaning.

Achieve is the closest. Both mean "to successfully complete a goal through effort." The difference is subtle: achieve leans slightly toward the result or outcome ("she achieved success"), while accomplish leans slightly toward the task being carried out and completed ("she accomplished the task"). In everyday speech, people use them interchangeably and that is perfectly fine — the overlap is enormous. But in precise writing, keep this nuance in mind.

Complete simply means to finish. It is neutral and carries no judgment about difficulty or meaning. "I completed the form" just means the form is filled in. It says nothing about a goal or effort.

Fulfill is about meeting an expectation, duty, or promise. You fulfill a promise, a role, or a potential — there is always a sense of something that was owed or expected being delivered.

Attain means to reach or arrive at a level or state — like a rank, milestone, or height. It often implies a journey upward.

None of these carry what "accomplish" carries: the specific sense of a meaningful task or goal being purposefully and successfully completed in full.

• "The scientist accomplished what no one had done before — a cure for the disease."
  • "Despite the tight deadline, the team accomplished all their targets."
  • "He worked all day but felt like he hadn't accomplished anything."
  • "What do you hope to accomplish this year?"
  • "The project was accomplished ahead of schedule."
  • "She accomplished her dream of becoming a pilot."

Notice how in each case, there is a clear intention + effort + completion.

Since you want to fully understand this word, here are the other forms you will encounter:

Accomplished (adjective) — This has two distinct uses:

  1. Skilled and refined: "He is an accomplished pianist." This means he has reached a high level of skill, usually through years of work. When you call someone "accomplished," you are saying they have mastered something.
  2. Done/completed: "The task is accomplished." — The passive form, meaning it's been completed.

Accomplishment (noun) — Also has two uses:

  1. Something you have achieved or done successfully: "Running a marathon was a great accomplishment."
  2. A skill or talent you have developed: "She has many accomplishments, including painting, piano, and cooking."

Unaccomplished (adjective) — Either not completed (a task left unaccomplished) or lacking skill or achievement (a person described as unaccomplished). This form is less common.

Using "accomplish" without an object. Unlike some verbs, "accomplish" generally needs a what. Saying "I accomplished" and stopping there sounds incomplete. You need to say what was accomplished: "I accomplished my goal" / "I accomplished a great deal." The one common exception is negative constructions like "I accomplished nothing."

Using it for accidental results. Because "accomplish" always implies intention, avoid using it for things that happened by chance or without a plan.

Thinking "accomplish" and "achieve" are 100% identical. They are very close, but when precision matters, remember: accomplish = completing a task; achieve = reaching a result.

"Accomplish" sits comfortably in the neutral-to-formal range. It works naturally in:

  • Professional writing: "The team accomplished all quarterly objectives."
  • Academic writing: "The research accomplished its primary aim."
  • Everyday conversation: "Did you accomplish much today?"

In very casual speech, people sometimes prefer phrases like "get done," "pull off," "manage to do," or "nail it" — but "accomplish" is never out of place in any of these settings.
To accomplish something means to successfully and intentionally complete a goal, task, or objective — all the way through, not just partly, and through real effort.
192:
When you call someone accomplished, you mean they are highly skilled at something — not just decent, not just average, but genuinely excellent, with a level of mastery that earns real respect and admiration.

Think of it this way: there are millions of people who can play the piano. But if someone says "She is an accomplished pianist," they are telling you that this person plays at a level that is polished, refined, and impressively high — the kind that makes you sit up and pay attention.
What Makes It Different From Just "Skilled" or "Good"

This is the key nuance, and it's important.

Skilled simply means you have ability in something. It is a neutral, factual word. A carpenter who builds decent furniture is skilled.

Accomplished carries something extra. It suggests:

  • A high degree of mastery, not just basic or moderate ability.
  • A sense of refinement and polish — the person does not just do something, they do it with a quality that reflects deep experience.
  • An achievement worth acknowledging — the word itself contains a quiet admiration. When you use it, you are saying this person's ability is something noteworthy.

So while every accomplished person is skilled, not every skilled person would be called accomplished.

"Accomplished" is a positive, admiring word. It is also slightly formal and elevated in tone. When someone is described as accomplished, it feels like a respectful compliment — the kind you might read in a biography, a professional introduction, or a formal recommendation.

If someone says, "Allow me to introduce Dr. Mehta, an accomplished surgeon," you immediately understand that Dr. Mehta is not just any surgeon — she is someone at the top of her craft.
How It Is Used — Patterns and Examples

The word almost always comes before a noun (the area of skill), describing a person:

  • An accomplished musician — someone who plays music at an impressively high level.
  • An accomplished writer — someone whose writing is skillful, polished, and well-regarded.
  • An accomplished athlete — someone who has achieved excellence in their sport.
  • An accomplished chef — someone who cooks with mastery, far beyond ordinary cooking.
  • An accomplished diplomat — someone who is highly skilled at the sensitive work of diplomacy.

You can also use it after a verb:

  • "She is accomplished in several languages." (skilled and proficient in them)
  • "He is widely accomplished." (skilled across several areas)
It Often Implies Effort and Dedication

"Accomplished" quietly suggests that the skill was earned over time through serious effort, practice, and commitment — not just stumbled upon. It is rarely used for things that come easily or casually. This is why the word carries weight: it honors not just the result (the skill), but also the journey behind it.
It Can Apply to Multiple Skills at Once

A person can be described as accomplished across several areas, which suggests they are a well-rounded individual of high ability. For example:

"She was an accomplished pianist, poet, and linguist."

This tells you that in all three areas, she had reached an impressive level of mastery — not just dabbled.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what the word does not mean:

  • It does not mean simply "finished" or "done" (that is the verb form — "The task was accomplished.") In the adjective form, it is always about a person's high level of skill, not about completing something.
  • It does not mean famous. An accomplished person may be completely unknown to the world, but still extraordinarily skilled in their field.
  • It does not mean perfect. It means highly skilled and impressive — but it is not an absolute superlative.
The Degree of Skill It Implies

Think of skill on a scale from 1 to 10. "Accomplished" typically refers to someone in the 7–9 range — clearly excellent and deserving of admiration, well above ordinary, but without necessarily claiming they are the single greatest in the world. It is a word of strong, genuine praise — not mild flattery, but also not over-the-top exaggeration.
A Final Summary to Lock It In

Accomplished describes a person who has reached a high, polished, and impressive level of skill in one or more areas — a level that reflects deep experience and serious dedication, and that earns genuine respect and admiration from others.

When you call someone accomplished, you are paying them a meaningful compliment. You are saying: this person is not just good — they are genuinely excellent, and their skill is something worth recognizing.
193:
An accomplishment is something you have successfully done, especially something that took effort, skill, or time. It is the result of trying to do something and actually doing it well.

Think of it this way: you set out to do something, you work toward it, and you succeed. That success — that finished result — is your accomplishment.

This word carries three related but slightly different meanings depending on how it is used. Understanding all three will give you complete command of the word.

Meaning 1 — A Completed Achievement (Most Common Use)

This is the meaning you will encounter most often. An accomplishment is something noteworthy that a person has successfully completed, especially when it required effort, persistence, or ability.

The key idea here is that it was not easy — there was a challenge involved, and the person overcame it. This is what separates an accomplishment from just any ordinary task you finish. You don't call making tea an accomplishment. But running a marathon? Writing a novel? Learning a new language? These are accomplishments.

Examples:

  • "Winning the championship was the greatest accomplishment of her career."
  • "Graduating from university was a proud accomplishment for him."
  • "Building a business from nothing is no small accomplishment."

Notice that the word carries a sense of pride and worth. When something is called an accomplishment, the speaker is saying: "This mattered. This was hard. This deserves recognition."

Meaning 2 — The Act of Completing or Achieving Something

Here, accomplishment refers not to the result, but to the process or act of getting something done. You will often see this used with the word "of."

Examples:

  • "The accomplishment of this mission required years of planning." (= the act of completing this mission)
  • "She dedicated her life to the accomplishment of her goals." (= the act of achieving her goals)
  • "The accomplishment of such a complex task surprised everyone."

In this sense, it is similar to saying "the completion of" or "the achievement of." You are describing the fact that something was brought to a successful conclusion.

Meaning 3 — A Skill or Talent (Almost Always Plural)

This meaning is slightly different and is most natural in its plural form: accomplishments. Here, it refers to skills, abilities, or areas of knowledge that a person has developed through learning or practice — things they are able to do well.

Examples:

  • "Among her many accomplishments, she speaks four languages and plays the violin."
  • "He listed his accomplishments on his résumé, including coding and public speaking."
  • "Drawing and cooking are two of her finest accomplishments."

In this sense, your "accomplishments" are your talents and capabilities — a picture of what you have mastered. This usage is common when describing a well-rounded, capable person.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Accomplishment" is almost always a positive word. It carries warmth, pride, and a sense of deserved satisfaction. When you use it, you are acknowledging that something real and meaningful was done — not just that a box was checked.

This is why you often hear the phrase "a sense of accomplishment" — the feeling of satisfaction and pride that comes when you complete something difficult or meaningful. This feeling is one of the most rewarding human emotions, and this word captures it precisely.

  • "Finishing the book gave her a deep sense of accomplishment."
  • "Even small wins can give you a sense of accomplishment."
Singular vs. Plural — A Subtle but Important Difference

Singular — "an accomplishment": Refers to one specific thing you have done or achieved.

  • "Getting promoted was a major accomplishment."

Plural — "accomplishments": Refers to a collection of things you have achieved or the skills and abilities you have developed over time.

  • "She has many accomplishments to be proud of."
  • "His accomplishments include decades of research and several published books."

When the plural is used to mean skills and talents, it often paints a picture of a person's overall capability and depth.
How It Compares to Similar Words

These words are close in meaning, but not identical:

Achievement is the most similar word to accomplishment. The difference is subtle: "achievement" is slightly more formal and often used in objective contexts (awards, records, data). "Accomplishment" feels slightly more personal and carries more emotional warmth. You'd say "a personal accomplishment" more naturally than "a personal achievement," though both are grammatically correct.

Feat suggests something extraordinary, almost impressive in a physical or daring sense — something that astonishes people. A feat is always exceptional. An accomplishment can range from modest to remarkable.

  • "Crossing the ocean alone in a rowboat was an incredible feat."

Skill (in Meaning 3) is the closest synonym when "accomplishments" refers to talents. However, "skill" is neutral — it just means the ability to do something. "Accomplishment" adds the implication that the skill was developed through effort and deserves recognition.

These fixed phrases will help you sound natural when using this word:

  • A sense of accomplishment — the feeling of pride and satisfaction after completing something meaningful.
  • A great / major / remarkable accomplishment — used to emphasize how significant the achievement is.
  • No small accomplishment — a phrase meaning "actually quite impressive," often used to acknowledge that something was harder than it looked.
    "Keeping the team motivated under pressure was no small accomplishment."
  • A lifetime of accomplishments — all the meaningful things a person has achieved over the course of their life.
  • List your accomplishments — commonly used in professional settings, such as on a résumé or in a job interview, referring to your achievements and skills.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

Meaning 1A specific thing you have successfully done, especially something difficult or meaningful.
Meaning 2The act or process of completing something.
Meaning 3A skill or talent developed through effort (usually plural).
ToneAlways positive — pride, satisfaction, and worth are built into the word.
Key phraseA sense of accomplishment = the warm feeling of having done something well.

The word "accomplishment" honours effort. It says: "This was not easy, and yet it was done." Whether it describes a finished goal, the act of reaching it, or the skills a person has built — it always carries respect for the work behind the result.
194:
Accord is about two or more things being lined up, matched, or in agreement — whether that's people agreeing on something, ideas matching each other, or a decision aligning with a set of values.

Think of it this way: when two puzzle pieces fit together perfectly, they are "in accord." Nothing is clashing. Nothing is out of place. Everything fits.

"Accord" carries a few distinct but closely related meanings. All of them revolve around that same central idea of agreement and alignment.

Meaning 1 — A Formal Agreement Between Parties

This is the most common everyday use. An accord is an official or formal agreement reached between two or more parties — often countries, governments, or organizations.

It is similar to words like treaty, pact, or deal, but "accord" often feels slightly less rigid and legalistic than "treaty." It suggests that the involved parties have come together, talked it through, and reached a mutual understanding.

Examples:

  • "The two nations signed a peace accord to end the war."
  • "After months of difficult talks, the leaders finally reached an accord on climate change."
  • "The company and the union came to an accord over wages."

A good way to remember this: an accord is what happens at the end of a long negotiation when everyone finally says, "Yes, we agree."

Meaning 2 — A State of Agreement or Harmony

Beyond formal agreements, "accord" also describes a state of being in harmony — when things, ideas, or people are consistent with each other, or when there is no conflict between them.

In this sense, it almost always appears in the phrase "in accord with", which means consistent with, matching, or in agreement with.

Examples:

  • "His actions were fully in accord with his values." (His actions matched his values — there was no contradiction.)
  • "The judge's decision was in accord with the law." (The decision was consistent with what the law says.)
  • "Her report was not in accord with the facts." (Her report contradicted or didn't match the facts.)

Notice how "in accord with" is a powerful, precise way of saying something is aligned with or not contradicting something else.

Meaning 3 — "Of One's Own Accord" (The Most Important Phrase)

This is a fixed phrase you absolutely must know. It means: doing something voluntarily, by your own free choice, without being asked, forced, or pressured by anyone.

The key idea is that the action came entirely from within the person — no one pushed them into it.

Examples:

  • "She apologized of her own accord." (No one told her to. She chose to apologize herself.)
  • "He left the job of his own accord." (He wasn't fired. He chose to leave on his own.)
  • "The dog came back home of its own accord." (No one called the dog. It returned by itself.)
  • "The child cleaned her room of her own accord, without being asked." (She just did it, unprompted.)

This phrase is extremely common in English, and getting it right is important. The moment you say someone did something "of their own accord," you are telling the listener: this was a free, personal choice — no outside force was involved.

Meaning 4 — "With One Accord" (Unanimously, All Together)

This is a somewhat more formal or literary phrase, but it's still used. "With one accord" means that a group of people did something unanimously — all together, as if they were a single person with a single mind. There was no disagreement, no holdout.

Examples:

  • "The audience rose with one accord to give a standing ovation." (Every single person stood up at the same time.)
  • "The committee rejected the proposal with one accord." (Not one member disagreed.)
  • "They all turned with one accord and stared at the door." (Every single person turned at once.)

Here is a summary of everything, in plain terms:

"Accord" (noun) always involves alignment, agreement, or harmony. Specifically:

  • As a formal agreement → Countries/groups sign an accord to settle something. (A peace accord. A trade accord.)
  • As a state of consistency → Something is "in accord with" something else when they match and don't contradict. (His behavior was in accord with the rules.)
  • As "of one's own accord" → A person acts freely, voluntarily, without being told to. (She came forward of her own accord.)
  • As "with one accord" → A group acts unanimously, all at once, with no disagreement. (They agreed with one accord.)
One Thing to Watch Out For

People sometimes confuse "accord" with "accordance." They are related but not the same.

  • "In accord with" = in agreement with, consistent with (slightly more about harmony between things)
  • "In accordance with" = in compliance with, following the rules of (slightly more about following procedures or rules)

For example:

  • "The plan is in accord with our values." ✅ (Our values and the plan are aligned.)
  • "The plan was carried out in accordance with the regulations." ✅ (The plan followed the regulations as required.)

In informal use, these are often interchangeable, but knowing the subtle difference will sharpen your writing.

That is the full picture of "accord" as a noun — every meaning, every key phrase, and every nuance you'll need.
195: "Accord" as a verb has two distinct meanings. They are related by a shared idea underneath — the idea of things fitting together — but they work differently on the surface.
Meaning 1: To give or grant something to someone

This is the most common use. When you accord something to someone, you give or grant it to them — but it's a specific kind of giving. The thing being given is almost always intangible: respect, recognition, trust, importance, rights, a privilege, a welcome, or status. And crucially, there is an underlying sense that the thing being given is appropriate or fitting — something the person deserves, or something that properly belongs to their position.

This is the key difference from just saying "gave." "Gave" is neutral. "Accorded" quietly carries the meaning of: this is what was proper or due.

Here are some examples:

  • "The committee accorded her the highest honor." — They gave her the honor, as was fitting for what she had achieved.
  • "He was not accorded the dignity he deserved." — He was not given the dignity that was rightfully appropriate to him.
  • "The king accorded the ambassador a formal audience." — The king granted the ambassador an audience, as was proper for someone of that role.
  • "The town accorded the returning soldiers a hero's welcome." — The town gave them a welcome that felt right and appropriate.

Notice you would never say "he accorded her a sandwich" — the word simply doesn't fit ordinary, physical acts of giving. It belongs to formal, significant, or ceremonial acts of giving abstract things.

You will also notice that "accord" in this meaning is very often used in the passive voice — "she was accorded great respect," "he was accorded a standing ovation" — because the focus is on what was given to the person, not on who gave it.
Meaning 2: To be in agreement or harmony with something

In this use, "accord" is always followed by the word "with." When something accords with something else, it means the two things are consistent, compatible, and non-contradictory — they line up with each other. If something does not accord with something else, there is a conflict or mismatch between them.

Think of it this way: you use this meaning when you want to check whether two things fit together without contradiction — like checking whether a person's behavior matches their stated values, or whether new evidence fits an existing theory.

Examples:

  • "His actions do not accord with his words." — His behavior is inconsistent with what he claims. They don't match.
  • "The new findings accord with the original research." — The new findings are consistent with and support the earlier research.
  • "This decision does not accord with our principles." — This decision goes against / is incompatible with our principles.
  • "Her account of events accords with what the witnesses described." — Her version of events is consistent with what the witnesses said.

The key nuance here: it's not just about two things being similar. It's specifically about whether they are compatible and non-contradictory. You'd use this meaning when asking: does this align with that? Does this fit?

Both meanings of "accord" are formal and literary. You'll find this word in journalism, academic papers, legal documents, formal speeches, and serious writing. In everyday casual conversation, people almost never say it — they would say "gave him respect," "showed her recognition," "doesn't match," or "doesn't line up with" instead.

So understanding "accord" as a verb is most useful for reading formal texts, and for writing in elevated or professional registers yourself.
The thread that connects both meanings

Even though the two meanings seem different on the surface, there is one idea underneath both of them: fitting together appropriately.

In the first meaning, something is given because it fits the person — it's appropriate to who they are or what they deserve.

In the second meaning, two things align because they fit each other — one is consistent with the other.

In both cases, "accord" is about a kind of harmony — things being in their right, fitting relationship with each other. Once you see that, the word starts to feel like a single coherent idea rather than two separate ones.
196:
Accordance is a noun that means agreement, harmony, or alignment between two or more things — where one thing matches, follows, or conforms to another.

Think of it this way: when two things are "in accordance," they are on the same page. They do not conflict. One lines up neatly with the other.

Here is something crucial to understand: the word accordance almost never stands alone in a sentence. It almost always appears as part of the fixed phrase "in accordance with."

"In accordance with" means: following, as required by, as guided by, or consistent with something — usually a rule, a law, a plan, a wish, a standard, or an agreement.

Think of "in accordance with" as a formal, precise way of saying "following" or "as stated/required by."

Here are examples that show the phrase in real situations:

Law and rules:
"The officer acted in accordance with the law."
→ The officer followed the law. Their action matched what the law required.

Instructions or plans:
"The project was completed in accordance with the original plan."
→ The project was done exactly as the plan said it should be.

Someone's wishes:
"In accordance with her wishes, the ceremony was kept private."
→ Because she wanted a private ceremony, that wish was respected and followed.

Company or official policy:
"Your application will be processed in accordance with our standard procedures."
→ Your application will be handled by following the normal steps and rules.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Accordance has a formal, official tone. You will most often see it in legal documents, official notices, policy statements, professional emails, and formal writing. It signals that something was done properly — that a rule, guideline, wish, or standard was respected and followed.

In everyday casual speech, people would simply say "following" or "based on" or "as per." But in formal contexts, "in accordance with" is the preferred, precise way to say the same thing.

When you say something was done in accordance with something else, you are implying there is a standard that existed beforehand, and the action or decision aligned with that pre-existing standard. There is no conflict, no deviation, no violation.

For example:

  • "The punishment was decided in accordance with the school's rules."

This tells you: the school had rules. The punishment did not go against those rules. Everything was consistent.

This is why the word is so common in legal and official language — it assures the reader that proper procedures were followed.

Occasionally, and mostly in older or very formal writing, accordance appears outside the phrase "in accordance with." In those cases, it simply means agreement or harmony between things.

For example:
"There was a remarkable accordance of opinion between the two scientists."
→ The two scientists' opinions were in agreement. They thought alike on the matter.

This standalone use is rare in modern English, so do not worry about it too much. If you master "in accordance with," you have mastered the word.

Whenever you see or hear "in accordance with," mentally replace it with "following" or "as required by" — the sentence will mean the same thing. If the replacement works smoothly, you have understood it correctly.

"Payments will be made in accordance with the contract."
= "Payments will be made as required by the contract." ✓

Accordance means agreement, harmony, or conformity. Its most important use is in the phrase "in accordance with," which means following or consistent with a rule, plan, law, wish, or standard. It carries a formal tone and is widely used in official, legal, and professional writing to show that something was done properly, without deviation from an established standard.
197:
"According" as an adjective means in alignment with, in agreement with, or in harmony with something else. It describes a relationship where two things correspond to each other — where one thing fits, matches, or conforms to another.

Think of it like a key fitting into a lock. The key is "according to" the lock — it matches it, aligns with it perfectly. That sense of correspondence between two things is the soul of this word.

"According" as an adjective behaves unlike most adjectives, and this is important to understand.

Most adjectives can sit before a noun:

  • "a happy child"
  • "a tall building"

But "according" never goes before a noun. You cannot say "an according decision" or "the according result." This would be wrong.

Instead, "according" appears after a linking verb (like is, was, went), and almost always immediately followed by the word "to":

  • ✅ "Everything went according to plan."
  • ❌ "The according plan succeeded." (this is incorrect)

This "according to" construction is the form in which you will encounter this word in virtually all of modern English. While traditional grammar classifies "according" as an adjective here, some modern grammarians treat the whole phrase "according to" as a compound preposition — that is, a two-word unit that functions the way a single preposition like "in" or "by" does. Both views are legitimate, and what matters practically is that you understand what "according to" means and how it works.

"According to" is versatile. It carries three distinct but closely related meanings. Knowing all three is essential.

Meaning 1 — "As stated or reported by [a source]"

In this use, "according to" introduces information and tells you where it comes from. It attributes a claim to an external source — a person, a document, a report, a study.

"According to the doctor, you need complete rest."

(= The doctor says this. We are citing the doctor.)

"According to the latest research, green tea may reduce inflammation."

(= This is what the research reports.)

"According to Maria, the project has been delayed."

(= Maria told us this.)

A very important subtlety here: when you say "according to [source]," you are not personally guaranteeing that the information is true. You are simply reporting what the source says. This is precisely why journalists and writers use it constantly — it allows them to report a claim while maintaining a neutral distance from it.

This also explains why you never say "according to me." Since "according to" always points to an external source, it would be contradictory to point it at yourself. When you want to express your own view, you say "in my opinion," "I think," or "as I see it" — not "according to me."

✅ "According to the report, unemployment is falling."
❌ "According to me, this is a good idea." (Use "in my opinion" instead.)

Meaning 2 — "In conformity with / in a way that matches [a rule, plan, or standard]"

Here, "according to" describes an action or outcome that follows or conforms to something — a set of rules, a plan, an agreement, a procedure, or an instruction. The idea is that the action aligns with the standard.

"The project was completed according to the client's specifications."

(= It met the specifications. It matched what was required.)

"Everything went according to plan."

(= Events unfolded exactly as the plan said they would. There was full alignment between the plan and what happened.)

"He was sentenced according to the law."

(= The sentence conformed to what the law prescribes for that crime.)

"The medication must be taken according to the doctor's instructions."

(= You must follow the instructions exactly. Your actions must match the instructions.)

Notice that this meaning implies a pre-existing standard — a plan, a rule, or a guideline — and it tells you that the action being described met that standard. The opposite scenario — when things go wrong — is expressed by saying something did not go according to plan.

Meaning 3 — "In proportion to / depending on / based on [a variable factor]"

In this use, "according to" expresses that one thing varies in response to another. As the second thing changes, the first thing changes with it. There is a direct, proportional relationship between the two.

"Students are grouped according to their age."

(= The grouping is based on age. Older students go into one group; younger ones into another. Age determines the grouping.)

"The salary is set according to experience."

(= More experience leads to higher pay. Experience is the determining factor.)

"Each person was taxed according to their income."

(= Higher income, higher tax. The tax is proportional to income.)

"Prices fluctuate according to supply and demand."

(= When supply falls or demand rises, prices go up. Supply and demand are what drive the prices.)

The key insight here is the idea of a sliding scale. One thing goes up, the other goes up. One thing decreases, the other adjusts. "According to" signals this dynamic, proportional relationship.
How All Three Meanings Share the Same Root

Although the three meanings seem different on the surface, they all express the same underlying idea that was there from the start: correspondence, alignment, or matching between two things.

  • In Meaning 1, the information aligns with (is attributed to) a source.
  • In Meaning 2, the action or result aligns with (conforms to) a rule, plan, or standard.
  • In Meaning 3, the outcome aligns with (is proportional to) a variable factor.

In every case, two things are in correspondence with each other. That is "according" at its core.

These two words are related but work very differently. Learners often mix them up.

"According to" (adjective + preposition) — points forward to an external source, rule, or factor, and describes alignment with it.

"She acted according to the rules." (= in alignment with the rules)

"Accordingly" (adverb) — points backward to what was just said, and means "as a result of that" or "in a way that fits what was just mentioned."

"The rules had changed, so she acted accordingly." (= She changed her behavior as a result of the rule change.)

A simple test: if you can replace the word with "as a result" or "therefore," use "accordingly." If you are pointing to a source, a rule, or a factor, use "according to."

"According to" is appropriate in virtually every context — casual speech, formal writing, academic work, journalism, legal language. It is one of the most versatile and widely used phrases in English.

However, in formal and academic writing, it carries particular weight in Meaning 1, because citing sources is central to those contexts. "According to Smith (2021), ..." is a staple of academic writing precisely because it attributes claims to their sources and keeps the writer from making unsupported statements.
An Archaic Form Worth Knowing: "According As"

In older English — literature from the 18th and 19th centuries, the King James Bible — you may encounter the construction "according as," which functions as a conjunction meaning "depending on whether" or "in proportion as."

"He shall be rewarded according as he has worked."

(= His reward will be proportional to his work.)

This form is essentially obsolete in modern English. You are unlikely to use it in everyday speech or writing. But if you read older texts, you will encounter it, and now you know what it means.
An Idiom to Know: "According to Hoyle"

You may hear the idiom "according to Hoyle," which means correctly, by the book, or following the proper rules. It comes from Edmond Hoyle, an 18th-century Englishman who wrote authoritative guides to card games. His name became synonymous with doing things by the rules.

"If you want to do it according to Hoyle, you need to follow every step precisely."

(= If you want to do it correctly and by the rules...)

The adjective "according" captures the idea of alignment — one thing fitting, conforming to, or corresponding with another. In modern English, it almost always appears as part of the phrase "according to," which carries three meanings depending on context: attributing information to a source, describing conformity to a rule or plan, or expressing a proportional relationship. It never appears before a noun. It is not interchangeable with "accordingly," which is an adverb meaning "as a result." Everything you encounter from this word in daily life — in newspapers, books, conversations, and formal documents — flows from this one central idea of correspondence and alignment.
198:
"Accordingly" is a word that connects what you do (or what happens) to a situation or piece of information that came before it. It always looks backward at something already said or known, and uses that as the reason or justification for what comes next.

It has two meanings that are closely related. Understanding both will give you the complete picture.
Meaning 1 — "In a way that fits the situation"

This meaning says: the situation is X, so the action matches X.

Think of it like adjusting a dial. The circumstances point in a certain direction, and your behavior or action is turned to match that direction. You are acting in a fitting, appropriate way given what you know or have been told.

Examples:

  • "The weather forecast warned of a storm, so she packed accordingly." — She packed in a way that matched the warning — warm clothes, a raincoat, and so on.
  • "He was told the meeting was formal. He dressed accordingly." — He wore formal clothes to fit what was expected.
  • "The general received new intelligence and updated the plan accordingly." — He adjusted the plan to correspond to the new information.
  • "She received a salary raise and began living accordingly." — She started spending and living in a way that matched her new income.

The core question this meaning answers is: "How did they act?" — Answer: In a way that matched the circumstances.

This meaning is used to show that something is the logical consequence of what was just stated. It connects a cause to its effect. You can almost always replace "accordingly" with "therefore" or "as a result" and the sentence will mean the same thing.

Examples:

  • "The bridge was found to be unsafe. Accordingly, it was closed to traffic." — Because it was unsafe → it was closed.
  • "He failed to meet the deadline. Accordingly, the contract was cancelled." — Because he failed → the contract ended.
  • "There had been no rain for weeks. Accordingly, the harvest was poor." — Because of the drought → the crops suffered.
  • "The evidence was overwhelming. Accordingly, the jury returned a guilty verdict." — Because of the evidence → the verdict followed.

The core question this meaning answers is: "Why did this happen?" — Answer: Because of what was just explained.
Are These Two Meanings Really Different?

They are closely related, and many sentences carry both at once. The difference is subtle:

  • Meaning 1 focuses on the manner of an action — how someone behaved to fit a situation.
  • Meaning 2 focuses on the consequence — what happened because of something.

In practice, "accordingly" often blends both ideas. It says: "Something happened, and as a logical and fitting result, this followed." That blending is natural and correct — it's part of what makes the word feel smooth and precise in formal writing.

"Accordingly" always implies a logical, reasonable connection. It is never used for random or unrelated events. The link between the situation and the outcome must make sense — it must feel like a natural result or a sensible response.

❌ Wrong: "It rained yesterday. Accordingly, I like pizza." (No logical connection)

✅ Right: "It rained heavily. Accordingly, the match was postponed." (Logical, reasonable connection)

This is what makes "accordingly" more precise than simply saying "and then." It says the next thing follows naturally and reasonably from what came before. It carries a sense of logic and cause-and-effect.
Where in a Sentence Does It Go?

"Accordingly" is flexible, but here are its three most common positions:

1. At the beginning of a new sentence (most common), followed by a comma:

  • "The regulations changed. Accordingly, all staff were retrained."

2. After the subject, in the middle of a sentence:

  • "All staff were accordingly retrained."

3. At the very end of a sentence:

  • "The situation was dangerous, and they responded accordingly."

The end-of-sentence position (example 3) almost always uses Meaning 1 — it signals that someone acted in a fitting way, without spelling out the details of how.

"Accordingly" is a formal word. You will encounter it most in legal documents, business writing, academic papers, formal reports, and news writing.

In everyday speech, people rarely say "accordingly." They use simpler words like "so" or "because of that."

  • Formal (written): "The application was incomplete. Accordingly, it was rejected."
  • Informal (spoken): "The application was incomplete, so it got rejected."
