This does not mean "accordingly" sounds strange — it just means it belongs in formal or semi-formal contexts. Using it in casual conversation would sound a little stiff.

For Meaning 1 ("in a fitting way"):

  • Appropriately
  • Correspondingly
  • In kind
  • Suitably

For Meaning 2 ("as a result"):

  • Therefore
  • Consequently
  • As a result
  • Hence
  • Thus

Knowing these synonyms helps you both understand "accordingly" in context and find alternatives when "accordingly" feels too formal for the situation.

You will very often see the phrase "act accordingly" (or "behave accordingly," "proceed accordingly"). This is extremely common and always uses Meaning 1. It means: do whatever is appropriate and fitting given the situation.

  • "Please read the safety guidelines and act accordingly."
  • "The manager was informed of the issue and proceeded accordingly."

This phrase is often used when the speaker doesn't want to spell out exactly what action to take — they trust that the listener will figure out the right response based on the information given.

Core ideaWhat follows is shaped by what came before — logically and fittingly.
Meaning 1In a way that matches/fits the situation (How did they act? → Appropriately.)
Meaning 2Therefore; as a result (Why did this happen? → Because of what was just said.)
RegisterFormal
Key ruleAlways requires a logical, reasonable connection between the two things.

In one sentence: "Accordingly" tells you that an action or outcome is a logical, fitting response to the situation or information that came just before it.
199:
To accost someone means to approach them and address them in a bold, intrusive, or aggressive way — especially when they haven't invited the interaction and don't welcome it.

The word almost always describes an unwanted, forceful confrontation. It isn't just about speaking to someone. It's about stopping them, getting in their space, and demanding their attention in a way that feels uncomfortable, threatening, or pushy.

Think about the difference between these two situations:

  • A friend taps your shoulder and says, "Hey, how are you?"
  • A stranger steps directly in your path on the street, blocks you, and starts demanding money or aggressively trying to engage you.

The first is a greeting. The second is accosting you.

The key ingredients are:

  • Someone approaches you — they come to you, often uninvited
  • They address or confront you directly — they make you stop and engage
  • The manner is bold, aggressive, or unwelcome — it isn't pleasant or mutual

This is important. "Accost" is never a neutral word. It always carries a negative charge — either threatening, unpleasant, or at least very forward and uncomfortable.

You would never use "accost" to describe a pleasant surprise encounter. You wouldn't say, "My old friend accosted me at the café." That would feel bizarre and wrong, because the word implies something unwelcome.

Even if no physical harm occurs, accosting someone is always described as an unpleasant experience for the person being approached.
The Spectrum: From Pushy to Threatening

"Accost" covers a wide range of intensity, but all versions share the same uncomfortable quality:

Mild end: An overly aggressive salesperson who blocks your path in a shopping mall, won't let you walk away, and keeps pushing their product in your face — that person is accosting you.

Middle ground: A stranger who confronts you on the street, gets in your face, and loudly demands to know why you looked at them — that is accosting.

Severe end: A mugger who steps out of a dark alley, stops you in your tracks, and demands your wallet — that is accosting you too, in its most threatening form.

The common thread is: you did not ask for this encounter, and the person approaching you is making you feel pressured, uncomfortable, or unsafe.

"Accost" is most naturally used when the person doing the accosting is a stranger or someone unfamiliar to the victim. The word carries the additional unsettling quality that this person had no relationship or standing to approach you that way.

While it can sometimes be used when acquaintances confront each other, the word feels most at home — and most accurate — when a stranger is involved.

The word can be used in active or passive voice:

Active voice (someone accosted another person):

  • "A man accosted her outside the station, demanding to see her bag."
  • "The drunk stranger accosted every passerby on the corner."
  • "He was accosting tourists near the market, trying to sell them fake goods."

Passive voice (someone was accosted):

  • "She was accosted on her way home by a group of men."
  • "He felt shaken after being accosted by an angry stranger in the parking lot."

Notice that "accost" is very commonly used in the passive voice because the focus is usually on the victim of the encounter — the person who was approached and made to feel threatened or uncomfortable.

To keep your understanding razor-sharp, here's what the word does not mean:

  • It does not simply mean to talk to someone or greet them.
  • It does not describe a mutual, voluntary, or friendly encounter.
  • It does not require physical assault — the confrontation is verbal and behavioral, though it may sometimes escalate to physical.
  • It does not imply that violence actually occurred — only that someone was approached in a threatening or highly intrusive manner.
A Mental Image to Lock It In

Picture yourself walking alone at night. Someone steps out from the side, plants themselves directly in front of you, and speaks to you in an aggressive or demanding way — leaving you no easy way to simply walk away.

That is accosting. The boldness, the unwanted intrusion into your space, the demand for your attention, and the discomfort or fear it causes — that is the heart of the word.

Accost means to approach and confront someone in a bold, aggressive, or unwelcome way — typically a stranger — forcing an interaction they did not invite and do not want. It always carries a negative tone, ranging from pushy and intrusive to outright threatening.
